en: I bow down to Govinda, the supreme bliss, the true Guru, who is the subject of all the established conclusions of the Vedānta, yet who is himself beyond the range of the senses. (1)

For living beings, birth as a human is difficult to obtain; more so than that is manhood, and more so than that is the status of a Brahmin. More than that is devotion to the path of Vedic dharma, and more than that is scholarship. Beyond this is the discrimination between the self and the non-self, followed by personal realization, and finally, abiding as one with Brahman.
Liberation is not attained by us without merits earned through hundreds of millions of births. // 2 //
These three alone are difficult to obtain, being caused by the grace of the gods:
human birth, the desire for liberation, and reliance upon a Great Being.
Having somehow attained the rare birth as a human, and even therein the state of manhood and the mastery of the Vedas,
that person of deluded intellect who does not strive for liberation from the self is truly foolish.
For he is a destroyer of the self; through his false grasping, he destroys himself.

Who indeed is there so foolish-minded that he would be negligent regarding his own true interest, having obtained this human body which is so difficult to find, and even therein, the state of manhood? (5)
Let the scriptures speak, let them worship the gods, let them perform rituals, and let them revere the deities;
yet liberation cannot be attained without the realization of the oneness of the Self.
It is not accomplished even within an interval of a hundred Brahmās.
For the Śruti clearly declares that there is no hope for immortality through wealth, since it explicitly states that ritual action is not the cause of liberation. (7)
Therefore, for the sake of liberation, the wise man,
having abandoned the desire for the pleasure of external objects,
should approach a teacher who is peaceful and great.
With his mind thus concentrated on the meaning taught by him, // 8 //
Having attained the state of being established in yoga through steadfastness in right vision, one should uplift oneself by means of the self when it is submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra. (9)
Having renounced all actions for the sake of liberation from the bonds of existence, let the wise and steadfast strive with diligence, remaining established in the practice of the Self. // 10 //
Action is for the purification of the mind, not for the apprehension of an object; the establishment of an object occurs through investigation, not by millions of actions. // 11 //
Through correct investigation, the ascertainment of the reality of the rope is established,
which destroys the fear and suffering arising from the delusion of a great serpent.
The certainty regarding the true meaning is seen through investigation and beneficial instruction;
it is not attained by bathing, nor by giving gifts, nor even by hundreds of breath-restraints.
Success in the fruit is especially prayed for by the qualified practitioner;
for in this case, the means—such as place, time, and so forth—are present as auxiliary factors.
Therefore, having approached a Guru who is an ocean of compassion and the highest among the knowers of Brahman, an inquirer into the reality of the Self must engage in investigation. (15)
An intelligent and learned man, skilled in discerning what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected, and characterized by the aforementioned qualities, is qualified for the knowledge of the Self.
Indeed, it is held that only one who is discerning, dispassionate, endowed with qualities such as tranquility, and desirous of liberation is fit for the inquiry into Brahman. (17)
In this regard, four means of accomplishment have been taught by the wise; when these exist, there is firm attainment, but in their absence, success is not achieved. (18)

First, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities is attained; immediately after that, dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits in this world and the next; then clearly, the perfection of the six qualities beginning with tranquility (śama), and finally, the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva). // 19 //
The firm conviction that Brahman is real and the world is illusory—this very thing is declared to be the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities. (20)
Detachment is that desire to abandon the objects of enjoyment, from the body up to Brahman, which are impermanent, through seeing, hearing, and so forth. (21)
The repeated turning away of the mind from the multitude of sense objects through the perception of their defects, and its steady abiding in its own true object, is called tranquility (śama).
The withdrawal of both types of sense organs from their respective objects and their stabilization within their own sockets is proclaimed as *dama* (self-restraint).
This non-apprehension of external objects by the functioning of the mind is the supreme *uparati* (cessation). // 23 //
The patient endurance of all sufferings without prior recourse to remedies, and free from anxiety and lamentation—that is declared to be *titikṣā*. // 24 //
Faith is defined by the wise as the firm conviction in the truth of the scriptures and the words of the teacher, by means of which reality is apprehended. (25)
The constant establishment of the intellect (buddhi) at all times within the pure Brahman is called its concentration; it is not, however, the pampering of the mind (citta). // 26 //

The desire to be liberated from the bonds beginning with egoism and ending with the body—all of which are imagined by ignorance—through the realization of one's own true nature, is the state of seeking liberation (mumukṣutā). // 27 //
Even this [wisdom], though of dull or middling form, when increased through dispassion, tranquility, and so forth, and through faith in the guru, gives birth to the fruit. // 28 //
But for one who possesses both dispassion and an intense desire for liberation, it is only in such a person that tranquility and the other virtues become meaningful and bear fruit. // 29 //
Where there is dullness regarding these two— dispassion and the desire for liberation—
there the appearance of tranquility and the like is merely like water in a mirage.
Among the collection of causes for liberation, devotion alone is the most weighty;
the investigation into one's own true nature is what is designated as devotion. // 31 //
Others have declared that devotion is the inquiry into the reality of one's own self.
One who is endowed with the aforementioned means and desires to know the truth of the self should approach a wise guru from whom liberation from bondage is attained. (32)
He was a learned master of the Vedas, free from vice, unassailed by desire, and the foremost among those who know Brahman;
he had ceased from worldly activity for the sake of Brahman, being as tranquil as a fire without fuel—a boundless ocean of causeless compassion, a kinsman to the virtuous who bow before him. (33)
Having propitiated that guru with devotion through humble prostrations, modesty, and service, and having obtained his favor, one should ask him about that which is to be known by oneself. // 34 //
O Lord, salutations to you, the kinsman of those born into this world;
O ocean of compassion, lift me up with the glance of your own benevolent eye, for I have fallen into the ocean of existence.
By means of a straight and extensive rain of the nectar of compassion. // 35 //
Scorched by the forest fire of the irresistible cycle of existence,
tossed about by the winds of misfortune,
and terrified, protect me who has sought refuge from death.
I know of no other refuge. // 36 //
The great and peaceful saints dwell there,
acting for the welfare of the world like the spring season; having themselves crossed the terrifying ocean of existence, they lead others across as well.
Even those who deliver others by means of no cause. // 37 //
This is the very nature of great souls that they are inclined by their own self to dispel the fatigue of others;
this moon itself [is cool], yet it is harsh like the sun— [only when it reflects its light].
It is said that he protects the earth when it is scorched by the heat of the sun.

O Lord, sprinkle this one who is scorched by the flames of the forest fire of worldly existence with the nectar-like words poured from the jar of your speech— words that are exceedingly cool, filled with the experience of the essence of Brahman-bliss, and pleasant to the ear.
Blessed are those who have been made worthy recipients and accepted by you at the very moment your gaze fell upon them.
How may I cross this ocean of existence? What is my destination, and what is the means? I know nothing at all; O Lord, have mercy upon me.
Bring about the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra. // 40 //
Beholding his own one who had come for refuge speaking thus,
scorched by the heat of the forest fire of saṃsāra,
[the Buddha] looked upon him with a gaze moistened by the essence of compassion.
The Great-Souled One would suddenly grant him fearlessness. // 41 //
The wise one [bestowed it] upon him who had approached for instruction,
who was desirous of liberation, who acted according to what was taught,
whose mind was tranquil, and who was endowed with peace.
One should impart the instruction on reality solely out of compassion. // 42 //
Do not fear, O learned one; for you there is no downfall.
There exists a means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, by which very means the ascetics have gone to its further shore.
I shall point out that very path to you. // 43 //
There is a certain great means that destroys the fear of saṃsāra;
by means of it, having crossed the ocean of existence, you will attain supreme bliss.
Through inquiry into the meaning of the Vedanta, the supreme knowledge arises;
by that, the ultimate destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra subsequently occurs.
The direct word of the Śruti declares that faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga are the causes of liberation for one who desires release;
indeed, for him who abides in these very things, [liberation follows].
Liberation is [freedom] from the bondage of the body imagined by ignorance. // 46 //
Indeed, from the union with ignorance, there arises for you, who are the Supreme Self, the bondage of the non-self, and from that alone comes transmigratory existence;
the fire of awakened consciousness born from the discrimination between these two [destroys it].
It shall utterly consume the effects of ignorance, root and all. // 47 //
The disciple said:
"O Master, please listen with compassion to this question which I am asking; having heard the answer from your own mouth, I shall have attained my purpose. (48)
What indeed is bondage, how did it come to be, how does it persist, and how is there liberation?
What is that which is non-self, what is the supreme, and what is the self?
How is the distinction between these two to be explained? Let this be told. // 49 //
The venerable Guru said:
"You are blessed; you have accomplished your purpose; your lineage has been purified by you, since you desire to become one with Brahman through liberation from the bond of ignorance. (50)
Sons and others exist as those who can liberate one from the debt owed to the father;
however, there is no one other than oneself who can liberate one from bondage.
The suffering caused by a burden placed upon the head and the like is warded off by others; however, the suffering produced by hunger and so forth cannot be averted by anyone except oneself. (52)
When a sick person follows a wholesome diet and takes medicine,
the attainment of health is seen for him, and not through any other action performed.
The true nature of reality is to be known by oneself alone through the eye of clear awakening, and not by means of a scholar;
it is like the true nature of the moon, which is seen by one's own eyes.
What is it that is known by others which is understood? 54.
Who, even in hundreds of millions of eons, would be able to liberate oneself from the bondage of the fetters of ignorance, desire, karma, and so forth, were it not for the Self? (55)

Liberation is accomplished neither through yoga, nor through Sāṃkhya, nor through ritual action, nor through sacred knowledge; it is established by the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, and not otherwise.
The beauty of form of a lute and its skill in playing the strings serve only to delight the people; they are not sufficient for universal sovereignty.
Eloquent speech, a torrent of words, skill in explaining the scriptures, and the erudition of the learned— these serve for enjoyment, but not for liberation.
If the supreme reality is not known, the study of the scriptures is fruitless;
even if the supreme reality is known, the study of the scriptures is fruitless. (59)
The web of words is a great forest that causes the mind to wander;
therefore, those who know reality must strive to realize the true nature of the self.
For one bitten by the serpent of ignorance, what is the use of the Vedas, the scriptures, the mantras, or medicines, without the medicine of the knowledge of Brahman? // 61 //
Just as disease does not depart without medicine and its name,
so one is not liberated by the word "Brahman" alone without direct experience.

Without dissolving the visible world and without knowing the reality of the self, how can there be liberation for men through words of "Brahman," which yield nothing more than mere verbal expression? (63)
Without having destroyed his enemies and without having attained the sovereignty of the entire earth, one does not deserve to be called a king merely by the word "I am the king. (64)

Just as the discovery of a treasure requires the testimony of a trustworthy person, digging, and the removal of stones and other obstructions above it, yet the treasure itself does not come out by mere words; likewise, Brahman is attained through the instruction of one who knows Brahman, along with reflection, meditation, and so forth.
One's own stainless reality, concealed by the effects of māyā, cannot [be realized] through fallacious arguments. // 65 //

Therefore, with every effort, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of existence, the wise should exert themselves by their own means, just as they would in the case of a disease or similar affliction. // 66 //
The question which you have asked today is considered most excellent by those learned in the scriptures;
it is like a concise aphorism, its meaning is profound, and it must be understood by those seeking liberation.
Listen attentively, O wise one, to that which is being uttered by me;
from hearing this, you shall be instantly liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Complete detachment from impermanent things is declared to be the primary cause of liberation;
following that are tranquility, self-restraint, and fortitude.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) is for those who have completely renounced all worldly activities. // 69 //
Then, through hearing, reflection upon that, and long, constant, and uninterrupted meditation on its true nature, the sage,
having attained the supreme state free from conceptual construction, becomes a man of realized knowledge.
Right here, one attains the bliss of nirvāṇa. // 70 //
That which is now to be understood by you—the discernment of the self from the non-self—is being correctly stated by me; having heard it, fix it within yourself.
It is endowed with these constituent elements (dhātus) known as marrow, bone, fat, flesh, blood, skin, and the inner membrane,
and with the feet, shanks, thighs, arms, back, and head.
This is employed with the primary and secondary limbs. // 72 //
That which is celebrated as "I" and "mine," the body—
the locus of delusion— is called "gross" by the wise;
it consists of ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
Those elements become subtle. // 73 //
Having combined with one another's portions and becoming gross, they are the causes of the gross body;
their constituent parts (mātrās) become its objects.
The five objects, beginning with sound, exist for the pleasure of the enjoyer. // 74 //
Those fools who are bound to these sense-objects by the extremely difficult-to-subdue noose of passion come and go,
moving up and down and high and low.
They were carried away with speed by the messenger of their own karma. // 75 //
Bound by their own respective qualities, the five [senses] met their destruction through the five objects beginning with sound:
the deer, the elephant, the moth, and the fish.
What man, adorned with five bees, is there? // 76 //
Through its defect, a sensual object is more intense than even the venom of a black cobra;
it destroys the consumer by its taste, and this one [the eye] destroys the beholder even by the mere sight. (77)

Only he who is liberated from the great noose of desire for sense objects—which is so difficult to cast off—is fit for liberation; no other is, even if he is a knower of the six systems of philosophy.
The crocodile of hope drowns those seekers of liberation who possess a mere initial detachment and are striving to reach the further shore of the ocean of existence, before they have even reached it.
Having seized him by the throat, he turned him back with force. // 79 //
He by whom the grasping known as attachment to sense objects has been struck down with the sword of profound dispassion goes to the further shore of the ocean of existence, free from all obstacles.

Know that for one whose intellect is not clear as they traverse the uneven paths of sense-objects, death assails them at every step; yet for one who proceeds by their own skillful means according to the instructions of beneficial, virtuous teachers, it does not.
Know for certain that the accomplishment of the fruit is effective; this is the truth. // 81 //
If you truly have a longing for liberation,
abandon sense objects from afar as if they were poison; [cultivate] contentment, compassion, patience, and uprightness like nectar.
Always worship those who are tranquil and self-controlled with great reverence. // 82 //
Every moment, having set aside that duty which is the liberation from the bondage created by beginningless ignorance,
this body exists for the sake of others; yet one exerts oneself in nourishing it.
He who becomes attached destroys himself by his own mind. // 83 //
He who, desiring to nourish his body, wishes to see the Self, goes to cross a river while grasping a crocodile with the thought that it is wood. // 84 //
Delusion alone is the great death for one who seeks liberation regarding the body and so forth; he by whom delusion is utterly conquered is worthy of the state of liberation.
Abandon delusion, that great death regarding the body, wife, children, and so forth;
having conquered it, the sages go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
This gross and contemptible body is a mass of skin, flesh, blood, sinews, fat, marrow, and bones, filled with urine and excrement. // 87 //
From the gross elements that have been quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta) by the force of past karma, this gross body has arisen as the locus of experience for the self;
its state is waking, because therein occurs the perception of gross objects. (88)
The individual soul itself, by means of its own self, engages with gross objects through the external senses— objects of diverse forms such as garlands, sandalwood paste, women, and the like.
Therefore, there is praise for his awakening of the body. // 89 //
Know that this entire external world of saṃsāra, which is the support for the person, is this gross body, like a house for a householder. (90)
For the gross [body], there are the properties of birth, old age, and death;
manifold states such as childhood and so forth;
and various conditions such as caste and stage of life, which are like many diseases.
The distinctions [of the bodhisattva] consist primarily in [their response to] honor, contempt, and great respect. // 91 //
The organs of perception are hearing, touch, sight, smell, and taste, so called because they provide cognition of their respective objects;
while speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ [are the organs of action].
The organs of action [are so called] because they are inclined toward actions. // 92 //
The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is designated as mind (manas), intellect (dhī), ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti), and thought (citta) according to its own functions; specifically,
the mind is so called due to its functions of volition (saṃkalpa), conceptualization (vikalpana), and the like.
Intellect (buddhi) has the property of determining the nature of objects. // 93 //
Here, from the conceit "I am," there arises the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti); and by the quality of pursuing one's own interests, there arises the mind (citta). // 94 //
This very *prāṇa* becomes *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna* through its own differentiation of functions and modifications, like gold or water. (95)
The five beginning with speech, the five beginning with hearing,
the five beginning with breath, the five beginning with the clouds, as well as intellect and the rest, ignorance, desire, and action.
They call the subtle body the "city of eight."
Listen to this body known as the subtle,
the *liṅga* born from the unquintuplicated elements,
which carries latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and experiences the fruits of karma.
Due to its own ignorance, the self has an adventitious limitation that is beginningless. // 97 //
The state of differentiation becomes his dream,
wherein he shines as nothing but himself;
yet in that dream, the intellect itself is as if waking.
By means of various latent impressions (vāsanā) belonging to the present time. // 98 //
Wherein this Supreme Self shines forth by Himself, having assumed the state of agent and so forth,
He who is the witness of all, limited only by the adjunct of the intellect.
It is not stained by even a trace of the karma produced thereby;
because it is unattached, for that very reason it is not stained in the slightest by actions performed through limiting adjuncts (upādhi). // 99 //
This characteristic of performing all activities belongs to the conscious Self, the Person, just as tools such as an adze belong to a carpenter; by that very fact, this Self remains unattached.
For blindness, dullness, and acuity are properties of the eye due to its excellence or deficiency;
likewise are deafness, muteness, and so forth.
The faculties such as hearing and so forth belong to the self that knows, but not to the self itself. // 101 //
Experts declare that activities such as inhalation, exhalation, yawning, sneezing, secretion, and the process of departure are the functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth.
Hunger and thirst are the two attributes of the vital breath (prāṇa). // 102 //
The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) abides within these— the eyes and other senses— as well as in the body— by means of the egoistic conceit "I am," through the light of its own radiance.
This should be known as the ego (ahaṃkāra), which conceives itself as the agent and the enjoyer;
through its association with the qualities such as sattva and the rest, it experiences the three states.
One is happy when sense objects are favorable and miserable when they are the opposite;
happiness and misery are properties of those [objects], not of the Self which is eternally blissful. (105)
For an object is dear because it serves the self, not by its own nature;
since the self alone is naturally the most beloved of all, therefore the self is eternally blissful and can never experience suffering. (106)
That bliss of the Self which is experienced in deep sleep as being devoid of objects is [confirmed by] scripture, direct perception, tradition, and inference while one is awake. (107)
The supreme power of the Lord, whose name is unmanifest,
is beginningless ignorance consisting of the three qualities;
this Māyā is to be inferred by the wise solely from its effects.
By which this entire world is brought forth. // 108 //
It is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it of the nature of both;
it is neither different nor non-different, nor is it of the nature of both;
for it is neither with parts nor without parts, nor is it of the nature of both.
Her form is most wonderful and ineffable. // 109 //

Just as the delusion of a snake is destroyed by the discernment of the rope, so too are Rajas, Tamas, and Sattva— well-known as the three qualities— destroyed by the realization of the pervasive Brahman, which is pure and non-dual.
His virtues are [known] by their celebrated effects. // 110 //
The power of distraction belongs to *rajas*, from which activity—
consisting of motion— has issued forth since ancient times; from this [power], attachment and the other afflictions constantly arise.
Suffering and the like are those modifications of the mind. // 111 //
Desire, anger, greed, hypocrisy, and the like;
envy, egoism, jealousy, and malice— these terrible qualities are the passionate (rājasa) attributes that constitute the activity of man.
Because this dust is the cause of bondage to that [object]. // 112 //
This power of the quality of darkness (tamas) is called *māyā*; by it, the reality appears to me otherwise.
This very [power] is the cause of the individual soul’s (*puruṣa*) transmigratory existence.
It is the cause for that which is inclined toward the power of distraction. // 113 //
Even one who is wise, learned, and clever, if he has been seized by the darkness of a vision of the self as being extremely subtle,
does not clearly understand it even when repeatedly and explicitly awakened; through delusion,
he perceives what is merely superimposed as real and clings to its qualities.
Alas, this is the powerful and great obscuration, the energy of most wretched darkness. // 114 //
Lack of cultivation, perverse cultivation, non-cultivation, or misconception regarding this [truth]—
one who possesses such associations will certainly not relinquish them.
The power of distraction exhausts [it] incessantly. // 115 //
Ignorance, laziness, dullness, sleep,
negligence, and delusion are the primary qualities of tamas;
impelled by these, one indeed knows nothing at all.
He remains just like one who is drowsy or like a pillar. // 116 //
The pure sattva is like water; nevertheless, when joined with those two [rajas and tamas], it becomes capable of movement,
wherein the reflection of the Self is mirrored.
It illuminates all that is insentient, like the sun. // 117 //
For a mixed-natured being, there arise qualities such as freedom from pride, the observances (niyamas), the restraints (yamas), and so forth,
as well as faith, devotion, and the desire for liberation.
And divine prosperity is the non-cessation of what is unreal. // 118 //
The qualities of a pure being are clarity,
self-realization, supreme tranquility,
contentment, rapture, and steadfastness in the Supreme Self.
By which one attains the essence of eternal bliss. // 119 //
This unmanifest, described as consisting of the three qualities (guṇas),
is called the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra) of the self;
deep sleep is its state of non-differentiation.
With the functions of all the senses and the intellect dissolved. // 120 //
The complete subsiding of all forms of cognition and the persistence of the intellect in the form of its seed-state is indeed what is called the perception of deep sleep.
This is because it is universally established in the world that "I do not know anything at all. // 121 //

The body, senses, vital breath, mind, ego, and so forth—all modifications; objects such as pleasure and the like; the elements beginning with space; and the entire universe—none of these [are the Self].
For all this, extending to the unmanifest, is indeed without self. // 122 //
Know that all this—illusion and the effects of illusion, from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the body—is unreal, devoid of the nature of a self, and like a mirage in the desert. // 123 //
Now I shall fully declare to you the supreme nature of the Self,
by the knowledge of which a person, liberated from bondage, attains absolute isolation (kaivalya).
There exists a certain Self which is eternally the substratum of the notion of "I," the witness of the three states, and distinct from the five sheaths. (125)
He who perceives the entire existence and non-existence of the intellect and its modifications throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, thinking "I am this"—he is the Self. (126)
He who perceives everything by himself, whom no one perceives, and who cognizes the intellect and so forth—this [Self] does not cognize that [intellect]. (127)
By whom this entire universe is pervaded, and whom nothing whatsoever pervades;
who is this formless one, before whom all this shines, and who shines following after that light.
By whose mere presence the body, senses, mind, and intellect function toward their respective objects as if impelled. (129)
By that whose nature is eternal consciousness, the objects beginning with the ego-sense and ending with the body, as well as pleasure and the like, are perceived just like a jar. (130)
This inner self is the ancient Person,
the experience of uninterrupted and indivisible bliss,
eternally of one form, and consisting solely of pure awakening.
By whom the Āsavas are impelled, they move according to their will. // 131 //
Right here, within the self of sentient beings, in the cave of the intellect,
in the unmanifest space,
the radiant light shines forth intensely like the sun in the sky.
Illuminating this entire universe with his own splendor. // 132 //
The Knower, following after the modifications of the mind and ego, and the actions performed by the body, senses, and vital breaths,
like iron following fire;
It does not move, nor does it undergo any transformation whatsoever. // 133 //
It is not born, nor does it die;
it does not increase, nor does it diminish; it is eternal and undergoes no change, even while this body dissolves.
It does not dissolve into space of its own accord, like a jar.

Distinct from both the primal nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikṛti), the Supreme Self— whose essential nature is pure consciousness, who illuminates this entire universe of being and non-being, and who is devoid of all distinctions— shines forth throughout the states of waking and the rest.
"I am myself"—thus [the Self exists] directly as the witness-form of the intellect. // 135 //
With a restrained mind, through the clarity of your intellect, know directly that "this is I" within yourself— this very Self of yours—
and [cross] the ocean of saṃsāra, which has no further shore due to its waves of birth and death.
O Foremost One, may you become one who has accomplished his purpose, abiding in the form of Brahmā.
In this regard, the notion of "I" with respect to what is not the self is the bondage of this person; acquired through ignorance, it is the cause for the onset of the afflictions of birth and death.
It is by means of this very [notion] that one regards this unreal body as real through the intellect of the self.
Like a silkworm, it nourishes, moistens, and protects [itself] with the objects as its threads. // 137 //

In one who is deluded by darkness, the cognition of "that" arises with respect to "this not-that," because of the absence of discrimination; indeed, just as the notion of a rope flashes forth regarding a snake, from that [delusion],
a vast multitude of misfortunes falls upon the one who grasps it.
Therefore, that which is a false grasping becomes bondage; listen, my friend! (138)
This power of concealment veils the Self, which manifests with infinite majesty through its unbroken, eternal, non-dual power of consciousness.
Consisting of darkness, like Rāhu [obscuring] the solar disc. // 139 //
When his own self, which possesses stainless and radiant splendor, has become concealed, the person, through delusion, conceives of the non-self body as "I"; consequently,
he binds himself with the cords of bondage such as desire, anger, and the like.
But the vast power of rajas, known as distraction, causes affliction. // 140 //
Having lost the awareness of its own self through being swallowed by the crocodile of great delusion, the intellect itself enacts various states as if they were its own qualities,
within the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with the poison of sense-objects.
Sinking down and rising up again, this one of evil intellect and contemptible destiny wanders about. // 141 //
Just as a mass of clouds produced by the sun's radiance expands, obscuring the sun,
so too does the ego-sense arising from the Self obscure the reality of the Self.
Likewise, having concealed itself, it manifests by its own power.
Just as a fierce, icy gale on a dark day thick with dense clouds afflicts those who have swallowed the light of the sun,
so does the wind of ignorance afflict one of deluded intellect when the self is enveloped by incessant darkness.
One whose power of intense distraction is great exhausts oneself with manifold sufferings. // 143 //
From these two powers alone has the bondage of the person arisen; deluded by them, he wanders about, mistaking the body for the self. (144)

The seed of that which grows from the soil of saṃsāra is ignorance; the sprout is the notion of the body as the self; the tendril is passion; the water is karma; the trunk is the body; the branches are the vital breaths;
the tips are the collection of sense organs; the flowers are the objects of the senses; and suffering is the fruit.
In this world, the individual soul (jīva) is like a bird that experiences various kinds of results arising from manifold karmas. // 145 //
This natural bondage to the non-Self is said to be rooted in ignorance, beginningless, endless,
and characterized by the sufferings of birth, death, disease, old age, and so forth.
It produces a continuous flow for that [mind]. // 146 //
It cannot be cut by missiles, nor by weapons, nor by wind, nor by fire;
it cannot be severed even by millions of actions,
except by the great sword of discriminative wisdom.
Through the clarity of the element, cool and gentle. // 147 //
For one whose mind is fixed solely on the authority of the Vedas,
steadfastness in his own duty leads to the purification of the self; for one whose intellect is thus purified, there arises the supreme realization of the Self.
By that very means, there is the total uprooting of saṃsāra. // 148 //
The Self does not shine forth, veiled by the five sheaths consisting of food and the rest,
which have arisen from its own power, just as water in a pond is hidden by a mass of moss.
Once that moss has been properly removed, the water appears pure; it immediately removes the torment of thirst and bestows supreme happiness upon man. // 150 //
Even when the five sheaths are negated, this pure one shines forth—the supreme, self-luminous, ever-new form, whose sole essence is eternal bliss. // 151 //
The wise person must effect the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self for the sake of liberation from bondage;
by that very means, having realized one's own nature as Being-Consciousness-Bliss, one becomes blissful.
Having discerned the inner Self— unattached and actionless— from the category of the perceptible, like extracting the inner core of a reed from its sheath,
and having dissolved everything therein;
He who abides as that Self is liberated. // 153 //
This body is born from food; it is a sheath composed of food. It lives by means of food and perishes when deprived of it—a mere heap of skin, flesh, blood, bones, and excrement.
This [self], being eternally pure, cannot possibly exist as an agent of its own accord. // 154 //
Even prior to birth and until death, this moment does not exist; it possesses the quality of being momentary and is of an indeterminate nature.
It is not a single entity, nor is it insentient like a jar, as it is clearly perceived [to be otherwise].
How can one's own self be a knower of the modifications of existence? // 155 //

The body, consisting of hands, feet, and so forth, is not the self, because life persists even when it is impaired, and because its various capacities are not destroyed; furthermore, it is neither that which is controlled nor the controller. (156)
The distinction of the Self from the body, its attributes, its actions, and its various states is established by itself, for the Self is the witness of all these and is eternally existent.
How could this heap of bones, smeared with flesh, filled with filth, and exceedingly foul, be its own knower, being itself of a different nature? (158)
Foolish people conceive the notion of "I" toward this heap of skin, flesh, fat, bone, and excrement;
one who is inclined toward inquiry perceives it as something entirely distinct from that.
One's own true nature is that which has become the ultimate reality. // 159 //
The cognition "I am the body" belongs to the ignorant; however, the notion of "I" regarding both the body and the living soul belongs to the wise,
the great-souled one who possesses discriminative knowledge.
The thought "I am Brahman" indeed [arises] regarding the true Self. // 160 //
O you of deluded intellect, abandon the notion of a self here in this heap of skin, flesh, fat, bone, and excrement;
[fix it] instead upon the non-conceptual Brahman, the Self of all.
Practice supreme peace; devote yourself to it. // 161 //
As long as a wise person does not abandon that sense of "I" which arises from delusion regarding the body, senses,
and so forth while they do not truly exist, for that long there is not even a mention of liberation for him.
Let him be one who perceives the ultimate limit of the system of Vedānta. // 162 //
Just as you have no notion of "self" whatsoever regarding a shadow-body, a reflected image, a dream-body, or a body imagined within the heart; [so it is with this body].
And let it likewise not exist in a living body. // 163 //
The notion of the body as the self is indeed the seed for the arising of the sufferings of birth and so forth for men of false intellect; therefore,
you must abandon it with effort.
But when the mind is relinquished, there is no hope for rebirth.
This vital breath (prāṇa), adorned by the five organs of action,
becomes the sheath consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya); it is by this that the sheath consisting of food (annamaya) is endowed with self and filled.
He engages in all activities. // 165 //
Nor is the self, consisting of vital breath— a modification of air—
either a goer or a comer like the wind moving within and without; for it perceives nothing anywhere, whether desirable or undesirable.
Whether it be one's own or another's, one is always dependent on something else. // 166 //
The organs of perception and the mind constitute the sheath composed of mind (*manomaya-kośa*), which is the cause of the conceptualization of objects as "I" and "mine";
it is powerful, being characterized by the mental construction of distinctions such as notions and the like.
Having filled that preceding sheath, he expands. // 167 //

Being piled up by the five priests that are the five sense-faculties, with the stream of clarified butter that is the sense-objects, it blazes intensely with the fuel of manifold latent dispositions (*vāsanā*).
The fire consisting of mind burns away conceptual proliferation. // 168 //
For ignorance does not exist apart from the mind;
indeed, the mind is ignorance, the cause of bondage to existence.
When that [mind] is destroyed, everything is destroyed.
When this has expanded, everything expands. // 169 //
In a dream, which is devoid of external objects, the mind alone creates the entire universe— including the enjoyer and so forth— by its own power; likewise,
there is no difference in the waking state either.
All this is merely an expansion of the mind.
At the time of deep sleep, when the mind has dissolved,
nothing at all exists, as is well known to everyone;
therefore, for a person, [the world] is merely imagined by the mind.
For him, cyclic existence does not exist in reality. // 171 //
The intellect is led away by the wind and is led back again by that very same wind;
bondage is conceived by the mind, and liberation is conceived by that very same mind.
Having conceived an attachment toward all objects, beginning with the body,
one binds the person with that quality like a beast;
thereafter, for the wise man, there arises a distaste for it, as if for poison.
It liberates that very mind from bondage. // 173 //
Therefore, the mind is the cause for this living being in the ordaining of both bondage and liberation;
the cause of bondage is the mind defiled by the quality of rajas.
It is the pure [nature] of liberation, free from passion and darkness. // 174 //
Therefore, for the wise seeker of liberation, the mind becomes pure through the excellence of the qualities of discernment and dispassion, and thus it leads to emancipation.
One must first become firm in those two. // 175 //
The mind is indeed a great tiger that roams through the forest lands of the sense objects;
let those virtuous ones who seek liberation not go there. (176)
The mind produces for the enjoyer all objects of experience, both in their gross and subtle forms,
as well as the distinctions of body, caste, stage of life, and birth.
Qualities, actions, causes, and effects are eternal. // 177 //
Having deluded this unattached conscious form and bound it with the body, senses, vital breaths, and qualities,
[avidyā] incessantly causes it to wander in the delusion of "I" and "mine."
The mind [is active] in its own functions and in the enjoyment of their fruits. // 178 //
The transmigratory existence of the person arises from the defect of superimposition;
this bond of superimposition is fashioned by that very [person] who is undiscriminating and possessed of the defects of *rajas* and *tamas*.
This is the cause of the suffering of birth and so forth. // 179 //
Therefore, the wise who perceive reality declare that the mind is ignorance, by which the entire universe is whirled about, just as a mass of clouds is driven by the wind. (180)
Therefore, one who desires liberation must strive diligently to purify that mind;
for when it is purified, liberation becomes as certain as a fruit held in the palm of one's hand. (181)
He who, with exclusive devotion to liberation, has uprooted attachment to sense-objects, renounced all ritual action,
and is steadfast in hearing [the scriptures] and other practices through pure faith;
He shakes off the nature of passion from his intellect. // 182 //
Nor can the supreme Self be of the nature of mind,
for it possesses a beginning and an end, because it is subject to transformation,
because its nature is suffering, and because it is an object.
For the seer is not seen as having the nature of the seen. // 183 //

The intellect (buddhi), together with the organs of perception and their respective functions, characterized by agency, constitutes the sheath consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya-kośa); it is the cause of the individual soul's transmigratory existence. // 184 //
The transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti) known as consciousness (vijñāna), possessing the power of reflecting the forms of objects that follow it,
is incessantly endowed with knowledge and action, thinking "I am."
One identifies intensely with the body, the sense organs, and so forth. // 185 //

This living soul (*jīva*), whose nature is the ego (*ahaṃsvabhāva*) from beginningless time, is the bearer of all worldly transactions; possessing its former latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it also performs actions (*karman*).
Meritorious and non-meritorious actions, as well as their fruits. // 186 //
Even while entering various wombs, he neither comes nor goes, neither descends nor ascends;
such is the nature of this very one consisting of consciousness while awake.
The states such as dreaming and the experience of pleasure and pain [are the results]. // 187 //
This extremely radiant sheath of consciousness is the constant conceit of "mine" regarding the body and so forth, the duties of the stages of life, actions, and qualities.
Due to the power of the supreme Self's proximity, this limiting adjunct (upādhi) arises for it; namely, that the notion of "self" transmigrates through delusion. // 188 //

This very Self, consisting of consciousness, which flashes within the vital breaths and in the heart as light, becomes the immutable agent and enjoyer when situated within limiting adjuncts. // 189 //
Having itself undergone the limitation of the intellect through the defect of identifying with it, it perceives that which is other than its own nature as being of a false essence,
even though it is itself the self of all.
[They are] distinct from [the self] by their own nature, like pots from clay. // 190 //
Indeed, by the power of its connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the Supreme Self manifests the attributes of those adjuncts as its own qualities,
just as fire, though itself unchanging, appears to possess the modifications of iron through its contact with it.
For the Supreme is eternally of a single form by its very nature. // 191 //
The disciple said:
Whether the state of being a living soul (jīva) for the Supreme Self occurs through delusion or otherwise,
since its limiting adjunct (upādhi) is beginningless, the destruction of that which is beginningless is not admitted.
Therefore, its state as a living being and its cyclic existence would be eternal; it could not cease. O venerable Guru, tell me: how can there be liberation for it? (193)
The venerable Guru said:
"O learned one, you have asked well; listen to that with attention.
An imagination deluded by error does not possess authoritative validity. (194)
But for that which is unattached, inactive, and formless, no connection with objects is possible without delusion, just as there can be no blueness and so forth in space. (195)
The state of being a living soul (jīva) attained through delusion by one's own seer— who is devoid of qualities, actionless, and whose nature is inward consciousness and bliss— is not real.
In the absence of delusion, [the object] does not exist, because it lacks the nature of a real entity. // 196 //
As long as there is delusion, so long does this [snake] exist; for that which is manifested by false cognition exists only during the time of delusion due to negligence, like a snake in a rope.
When delusion is destroyed, even the snake does not exist; it is just like that. // 197 //
The beginninglessness of ignorance is likewise accepted for its effects; however, once knowledge has arisen, that which is illusory ceases, even though it was beginningless.
Upon awakening, everything—including its root—is destroyed like a dream;
though beginningless, this world is clearly not eternal, just like a prior non-existence. (199)
Even for that which is beginningless, the destruction of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is observed;
this [destruction] is conceptually constructed in relation to the self through its connection with the limiting adjunct of cognition (buddhyupādhi). // 200 //

The state of being a living soul is not something other than that [consciousness], nor is it distinct from its own nature; rather, the connection between the self and the intellect is preceded by false knowledge. (201)
The cessation of that [ignorance] occurs through right knowledge and not otherwise;
the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self is considered right knowledge by the Śruti. (202)
That [liberation] is accomplished only through the correct discrimination between the Self and the non-Self;
therefore, one must practice the discrimination between the inner self and the eternal Self. (203)
Just as water, though completely obscured by mud, becomes clearly manifest when the mud has departed, so too the Self shines with clear radiance when defects are absent. (204)
If, however, it were non-existent, there would clearly be a perception of this internal [object] as having the nature of existence;
therefore, its rejection must indeed be carried out.
[It is] always [the cause] of the self, of the virtuous person, and of such things as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). // 205 //

Therefore, this other self cannot be designated by the term "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya), because it is subject to modification, is insentient, and because of the reason that it is limited; furthermore, since it is an object of perception and is inconstant, it is not accepted as eternal. // 206 //

When its body is kissed by the reflection of bliss, the state of existence expands through the unfolding of darkness; it becomes composed of bliss, characterized by qualities such as "the beloved," and arises from the attainment of one's desired object.
Upon the experience of merit, for the wise, it shines forth spontaneously in the form of bliss itself.
Everyone who possesses a body rejoices therein without effort; that is truly excellent.

The manifestation of the sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa) is intense during deep sleep, whereas in dreaming and waking it is slight, occurring only in conjunction with the sight of desired objects. (208)
This supreme Self is not composed of bliss, because it possesses adjuncts, because it is a modification of primordial nature (prakṛti),
and because of the reason that it is an effect of well-performed action.
Because it is composed of an aggregate of transformations. // 209 //
When even the five sheaths have been negated through reasoning and scripture,
that which remains as the witness until their final negation is the nature of pure consciousness.
This Self, which is self-luminous, distinct from the five sheaths,
the witness of the three states, changeless, untainted, and eternally blissful— He should be known as one's own Self by the wise man. (211)
The disciple said:
"O Guru, since these five sheaths have been negated as being false, I perceive nothing here at all except for the total absence of everything."
Is there, then, any object to be known by the wise one through his own self-nature? 212
The venerable Guru said:
"You have spoken the truth; you are skilled in discernment.
The ego and other modifications are yours, and this absence [of them] is likewise dependent upon you."
Know that Knower, the Self, by means of a very subtle intellect—that which experiences all [objects] yet is itself not experienced. (214)
Whatever is experienced by anyone must have that [experience] as its witness;
for one who has not experienced a particular object, the status of being a witness is of no use.
This entity has itself as its witness because it is experienced by itself;
beyond this, the inner self (pratyagātman) alone is the direct witness, and nothing else.
Know that which flashes forth as the self of eternal bliss-consciousness to be this very Self within your heart. // 217 //
Just as a fool, seeing the reflection of the sun's orb in the water of a jar, thinks it is the sun itself;
so too [one mistakes] the reflection of consciousness situated within its limiting adjuncts.
Through delusion, the dull-witted person conceives the notion "I am."
Setting aside the jar, the water, and the reflection of the sun within it, one perceives the sun alone,
standing apart as the illuminator of this triad.
It is self-luminous, just as it is for the wise person. // 219 //
Having thus cast off the body and the intellect— which is but a reflection of consciousness— into the intellect deposited within the cave of the heart,
one perceives the Self as the seer, whose nature is indivisible awareness.
It is the illumination of all things, distinct from both existence and non-existence.
Having correctly realized this as one's own true nature— eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, extremely subtle, empty within and without, and non-dual from the Self.
The person is free from evil, free from passion, and free from death. // 221 //
Free from sorrow, a mass of bliss, and all-knowing,
he himself fears nothing whatsoever;
there is no other path to liberation from the bondage of existence.
Without the realization of one's own true nature, for one who desires liberation. // 222 //
The realization of non-difference from Brahman is the cause of liberation from worldly existence, by which the wise attain the non-dual bliss of Brahman. (223)
But the wise man who has become Brahman does not return again to the cycle of worldly existence;
therefore, one must correctly realize the non-difference of the Self from Brahman.
Victorious is Brahman—truth, knowledge, and infinite; pure, supreme, and self-established; whose singular essence is eternal bliss; non-different from the inner self; and uninterrupted. // 225 //
This is indeed supreme non-duality because of the absence of any entity other than itself;
for when one has attained the state of awakening to the reality of the ultimate truth, nothing else whatsoever exists. (226)
This entire universe, perceived in its various forms due to ignorance, is in reality nothing but Brahman, from which all defects of conceptualization have been cast away. // 227 //
Although the jar is an effect of clay, it is not distinct from the clay; for everywhere, apart from the nature of the clay,
there exists no jar-form separate from the jar itself.
How could that which is a mere falsely imagined name [be real]? // 228 //
No one can demonstrate the true nature of a jar by means of its being distinct from clay;
therefore, the jar is merely imagined through delusion.
The clay alone is real, being the ultimate reality. // 229 //
The entire universe is the effect of the True Brahman; it is Being alone, consisting of that alone, and there is nothing other than that.
He who says "it exists" [in this sense] has no delusion.
Having emerged, he spoke as if still asleep. // 230 //
"The Veda is indeed Brahman alone"— thus speaks the most excellent Vedic utterance established in the Atharva;
therefore, this entire universe is indeed nothing but Brahman.
There is no difference between the substratum and that which is superimposed upon it. // 231 //
If this world were real, there would be a loss of the infinity of the Self, the lack of authority for the Vedas,
and even the quality of being a speaker of untruth would belong to the Lord.
These three are not beneficial or wholesome for great-souled ones. // 232 //
"The Lord knows the true nature of things, yet I am not established in them;
nor do all beings abide in me"—thus indeed did he reflect.
If the universe were real, it would be perceived during deep sleep;
since nothing at all is perceived then, it is therefore unreal and false, like a dream.
Therefore, the world does not exist apart from the Supreme Self; its perception as separate is false, like [the appearance of] qualities and so forth.
For that which is superimposed, how can there be any purposefulness?
In the same way, the locus appears through delusion. // 235 //

If that which is perceived by one who is deluded is indeed nothing but delusion— just as mother-of-pearl is [mistaken for] silver— then Brahman is always conceptualized as "this" through such delusion.
It is merely a name superimposed upon Brahman. // 236 //
Beyond this is Brahman— real, non-dual, a mass of pure consciousness, stainless, profoundly tranquil, devoid of beginning or end, and actionless.
Its essential nature is the taste of uninterrupted bliss. // 237 //
It is that in which all distinctions created by māyā have been cast out; it is eternal bliss, partless, immeasurable,
formless, unmanifest, ineffable, and imperishable.
This light shines forth as something of its own accord. // 238 //
The wise know the supreme reality to be devoid of knower, known, and knowledge, infinite, free from conceptual construction, and pure, indivisible consciousness alone. // 239 //
I am Brahman—the full, great radiance; that which is neither to be abandoned nor to be accepted, beyond the range of mind and speech, immeasurable, and without beginning or end.
If, after both Brahman and the Self have been purified as denoted by the two words *tat* and *tvam*,
the Śruti correctly [declares] their identity with the words "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*),...
Unity alone is repeatedly established [in this way]:
the oneness of those two, which are indicated and not directly expressed,
and which possess mutually contradictory attributes, is declared.
Like a firefly and the sun, or a king’s servant;
like a well and the ocean, or an atom and Mount Meru. // 242 //
This opposition between the two is constructed by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and is not real;
this adjunct is the Lord’s māyā, the cause of the mahat and the rest.
Listen to the five sheaths, which constitute the function of the individual soul. // 243 //
These two are the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the Supreme and the individual soul;
when they are properly dispelled, there is neither Supreme nor individual soul—
just as there is neither king nor soldier for a monarch's sword.
When both of these are excluded, there is neither a soldier nor a king.
Furthermore, the Śruti itself negates the duality imagined within Brahman in the passage, "Now, therefore,
the instruction," through a realization supported by the authority of the Śruti.
Therefore, the rejection of these two must indeed be carried out. // 245 //
"This is not this, this is not that," because it is imagined, it is not real—
like a snake seen in a rope, or like a dream;
having thus eliminated the visible world through sound reasoning.
The single nature that exists between those two should be understood subsequently. // 246 //
Therefore, those two [terms] are well-indicated by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sake of establishing their indivisible single essence;
they are capable neither through exclusion (*jahatyā*) nor through non-exclusion (*ajahatyā*).
However, it must necessarily consist of both meanings. // 247 //
Just as in this world, the identity expressed by "This is Devadatta" is stated by setting aside the aspects of contradictory attributes,
so it is in the sentence "That thou art."
Having abandoned both [positions] due to the presence of contradictory properties. // 248 //
By perceiving the eternal self and consciousness as pure consciousness alone, the undivided state is realized by the wise;
thus it is declared by hundreds of great sayings.
The oneness of Brahman and the Self is the state of indivisibility. // 249 //
Having negated non-existence by means of the phrase "not gross," that which is established by itself as being like space and beyond ratiocination is therefore perceived as this mere illusion.
Abandon that which was grasped as your own self;
with a purified intellect, realize your own Self as the indivisible consciousness, simply as "I am Brahman. (250)
Just as every effect of clay, such as a jar and the like, is always established as being nothing but clay alone,
so too this entire world, produced from Being, is always of the nature of Being and is nothing but Being alone;
because there is nothing whatsoever beyond Being, that Being is the Truth, it is the Self, and it is itself.
Therefore, you are That—the supreme Brahman, which is tranquil, stainless, and non-dual.
Just as all things— the knower, the objects, and the space and time imagined during sleep— are false, so too is this world here in the waking state, because it is an effect of one's own ignorance;
for this reason, even this body, the senses, the vital breaths, and the ego are unreal.
Therefore, "That thou art" refers to that which is the supreme Brahman—tranquil, stainless, and non-dual.
That which is imagined through delusion is, upon its discernment,
found to be nothing other than that [reality] itself and not distinct from it;
just as the manifold world of a dream vanishes within the dream itself.
Is anything indeed seen as distinct from itself upon awakening? // 253 //
That which transcends birth, policy, family, and lineage; which is devoid of name-and-form and of qualities or defects;
and which extends beyond space, time, and objects.
Meditate upon the reality of Brahman within yourself: "Thou art That. // 254 //
That which is supreme, beyond the range of all speech, yet within the range of the eye of pure awakening;
that beginningless reality which is a mass of pure consciousness.
Meditate upon the reality of Brahman within yourself: "Thou art That. // 255 //
There exists that which is free from the six waves, cultivated within the heart of the yogi, not manifested by the sense organs,
unknowable by the intellect, and faultless.
Meditate upon the reality of Brahman within yourself: "That art thou. // 256 //
That which is the substratum for the portions of the world imagined through delusion, yet has itself as its own substratum; which is distinct from both being and non-being;
and which is indeed partless and beyond comparison.
Meditate upon the reality of Brahman within yourself: "Thou art That. // 257 //
It is imperishable, devoid of birth, growth, transformation, decay, disease, and destruction;
it is the cause of the creation and maintenance of the universe.
Meditate upon the reality of Brahman within yourself: "That art thou. // 258 //
That which is free from the eightfold divisions, whose defining characteristics are never cast aside, as motionless as a waveless ocean,
eternally liberated, and of undivided form;
Meditate upon the reality of Brahman within yourself: "Thou art That. // 259 //
The One Reality alone is the manifold cause;
it is the cause that dispels other causes,
and it itself is distinct from both effect and cause.
Meditate upon the reality of Brahman within yourself: "That art thou. // 260 //
That which is non-conceptual, immeasurable, and imperishable, distinct from both the perishable and the imperishable, supreme, eternal, immutable bliss, and stainless.
Meditate upon the reality of Brahman within yourself: "Thou art That. // 261 //
That which shines as the existent in manifold ways through the transformations of name, form, quality, and self due to delusion,
is itself always changeless, like gold.
Meditate upon the reality of Brahman within yourself: "That art thou. // 262 //
That which he desires— beyond the beyond,
the innermost essence of a single flavor, characterized as the Self,
true, consciousness, bliss, infinite, and immutable.
Meditate upon the reality of Brahman within yourself: "That art thou. // 263 //
One should personally contemplate this explained meaning within oneself with an intellect employing well-known reasonings,
until it becomes as free from doubt and the like as water held in the palm of one's hand.
By that, there will be a penetration of reality. // 264 //
Having realized that mere perfect awakening is the completely pure reality,
he always remains established within his own self, taking refuge in it as a king does in his army within the Saṅgha.
Dissolve all that is born in the universe into Brahman. // 265 //
Within the cave of the intellect, there exists Brahman— real, distinct from both being and non-being, supreme, and without a second;
he who dwells here within that cave as the Self [attains it].
Furthermore, there is no further entry into the cave of his limbs. // 266 //

Even when the true nature of reality is known, this beginningless and powerful latent impression remains firm— the notion that "I am the doer and the enjoyer"— which is the cause of this transmigratory existence;
it must be removed with effort by one who dwells within the Self through the vision of the inner witness.
The sages declare that liberation in this world is the attenuation of latent impressions.
The notion of "I" and "mine" regarding the non-self, such as the body and the senses—this superimposition must be discarded by the wise person through steadfast abidance in the Self. (268)

Having realized your own inner self as the witness of the intellect and its modifications, abandon the notion of "I" with respect to the non-self through the practice of right conduct, thinking simply, "I am That."
Having abandoned conformity with the world, having abandoned conformity with the body,
and having abandoned conformity with the scriptures, effect the removal of self-superimposition.
Due to the worldly impression, the impression of the scriptures, and the impression of the body, knowledge does not arise in its true form for a living being. (271)
Those who know the truth say that for one desiring liberation from the prison of saṃsāra, the three sharp latent tendencies (vāsanās) are like iron chains binding the feet.
He who is liberated from this attains liberation. // 272 //
Through contact with water and other substances, the divine fragrance of agallochum, though previously overwhelmed by a powerful stench,
shines forth perfectly through friction alone.
When the external odor is being shaken off. // 273 //
The self-impression (*ātmavāsanā*), which is otherwise excessively smeared by the dust of infinite, deep-seated, and far-reaching latent tendencies (*vāsanā*),
becomes utterly purified through the intense friction of wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is clearly perceived, like the fragrance of sandalwood. // 274 //

When the latent impressions of the self are obscured by the web of latent impressions of non-self, they vanish through steadfastness in the eternal Self; then, it shines forth clearly of its own accord. // 275 //
To the extent that the mind is established within itself,
to that same extent it relinquishes external latent impressions; when there is the complete release of these impressions, [the state of liberation is attained].
The self-experience is free from obstruction. // 276 //

By remaining always established in one's own self alone, the mind of the yogi perishes; and from this comes the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā). Therefore, effect the removal of superimposition upon the Self.
Darkness is destroyed by the two [qualities], passion by goodness, and goodness by the pure;
therefore, relying upon goodness, effect the removal of false attribution.
Having resolved that the body merely sustains what has already begun [its course], remain steadfast;
and by relying on fortitude with effort, bring about the removal of false superimposition.

"Realize that 'I am not the individual soul, but the Supreme Brahman'—first by means of the exclusion of what is not that [Self], and then remove the superimposition that has arisen through the force of latent impressions. (280)
Having realized the universal selfhood of the Self through scripture, reasoning, and personal experience,
effect the removal of superimposition wherever it appears by means of its manifestation.
For the sage, there is no action whatsoever through either grasping or relinquishing; by constant devotion to that alone, effect the removal of self-identification with the body. 282.

Through the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self arising from such statements as "That thou art," effect the removal of your own superimposition in order to establish firmness in the sense that the Self is Brahman. (283)
Until the ego-sense has completely dissolved within this body, remain vigilant and, with a disciplined mind, effect the removal of false superimposition.
O wise one, as long as the perception of the living world appears like a dream, for that long you must incessantly effect the removal of this superimposition.
Without giving any occasion for sleep, worldly talk, or even the forgetting of sounds and other sense-objects, contemplate the Self within the self.

Having abandoned this body produced from the impurities of your parents—a body consisting of filth and flesh—become like a Brahmin and, having become perfected, remain far away from it as you would from an outcaste. 287.
Having dissolved the individual self into the Supreme Self—just as the space within a jar merges into the great universal space—remain forever silent in a state of indivisible oneness, O Sage. (288)

Having become self-existent as the Self, let one abandon even the macrocosm of Brahmāṇḍa and the microcosm of Piṇḍāṇḍa—both being the self-luminous substratum—as if they were mere vessels of impurity. (289)
Having established the notion of "I" within the conscious Self, which is eternally blissful, and having cast off the subtle body (liṅga), remain forever as the absolute alone. // 290 //
Realizing that "I am that Brahman wherein this appearance of the world exists, like a city within a mirror," you will have accomplished all that is to be done.
Having approached that which is the true, primordial, non-dual consciousness-bliss— formless and actionless— one's own essential nature—
one should cast off this false body.
Like an actor, he has assumed a disguise for himself. // 292 //
This entire visible world is false in every respect; it is not the referent of "I," because momentariness is observed.
The cognition "I know everything" [is likewise false].
How could I be established as momentary from the very beginning? // 293 //
The referent of the word "I," however, is the witness of the "I" and so forth,
because it is observed to exist even during deep sleep;
for the Śruti itself declares, "He is unborn and eternal."
That inner self is distinct from both being and non-being. // 294 //
The knower of all transformations among those things that undergo change must itself be eternally unchanging;
this is evident in the states of desire, dream, and deep sleep.
The non-existence of these two has been seen again and again. // 295 //
Therefore, abandon the conceit regarding this lump of flesh, which is merely a conceptual construction of the intellect; instead,
take refuge in the indivisible awakening that remains unimpeded throughout the three periods of time.
Having known your own self, attain peace. // 296 //

Abandon pride regarding family, lineage, name, form, and stage of life— all of which rest upon a corpse still moist with decay— and likewise abandon the attributes of the outward mark, such as agency and the like.
Having abandoned [existence], he is the very nature of unbroken bliss. // 297 //
Other obstacles are seen to exist for a person that cause saṃsāra; of these, egoism (ahaṃkāra) is the first transformation and thus the root. // 298 //
As long as there remains a connection with one's own wicked ego, so long there will not be even a trace of the extraordinary news of liberation. (299)
Freed from the grasp of egoism, one attains one's true nature:
stainless like the moon, full, eternally blissful, and self-luminous. // 300 //
Or rather, when that which was previously perceived by the intellect as "I am he" is constructed by utterly deluded ignorance,
and that very [self] is destroyed without remainder; [then...]
The self-nature of Brahmā is free from obstruction. // 301 //

The treasure-trove of the bliss of Brahman is guarded within oneself by the terrible serpent of egoism, which possesses great strength; it is coiled around by its three fierce heads composed of the gunas.
Having severed these three heads with the great sword called higher knowledge (vijñāna), which is equipped with the ears [of learning], one attains liberation.
The wise person is capable of enjoying this treasure, which brings happiness and has its enemies eradicated. // 302 //
Just as whatever manifestation of the poison of venom exists in the body might lead to health [through its transformation], so too does the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) lead to the liberation of the yogin.

Through the absolute cessation of the ego and the withdrawal of the various conceptual constructions produced by it, one attains the reality [of the Self] as "I am this" through the discernment of the innermost essence. // 304 //
Suddenly abandon the notion of "I" toward the ego, which is the agent, which is of the nature of transformation, which reflects the self, and which robs one of one's own true state;
for it is through superimposition upon this that you have obtained a life abounding in birth, death, old age, and suffering.
Even for you, whose form is consciousness and whose body is bliss, this is the cycle of worldly existence.
Of you, the all-pervading Self of consciousness, whose form is eternally one, who is the embodiment of bliss, whose fame is faultless,
and who is never otherwise nor subject to change— of you, there is no alteration anywhere at any time.
Without superimposition upon me, there is no transmigratory existence for him.
Therefore, having clearly severed this ego— the self-enemy perceived like a thorn in the throat of the enjoyer— with the great sword of discernment, [one should proceed].
Enjoy the happiness of your own sovereignty as you desire. // 307 //
Then, having turned back from worldly activity from the very beginning and having abandoned all passion through the attainment of the ultimate truth,
I remained silent, experiencing the bliss of my own self.
With his full self, he is free from conceptual construction within Brahman. // 308 //
Even if this great "I" has been cut down at its very root, if it is once again scratched by the mind for even a moment,
it comes back to life and creates hundreds of distractions.
Just as a rain-cloud by the wind during the monsoon season. // 309 //
Having restrained the enemy within, one must never grant it any opportunity through preoccupation with sense objects;
for that very thing is the cause of its revival.
Like water from a jambīra tree that has withered away. // 310 //
How could one who exists as the body-self, being desirous,
be a desirer distinct from it? Therefore, [the state of] being intent upon the pursuit of objects is precisely what constitutes desire.
Through the occurrence of differentiation, it becomes the cause for bondage to existence. // 311 //
The increase of the seed is observed through the expansion of its effect;
the destruction of the seed follows from the destruction of its effect; therefore, one should bring the effect to cessation. // 312 //
From the increase of latent impressions (vāsanā) comes the effect, and from the increase of the effect comes the latent impression;
thus, for a person, saṃsāra increases in every way and does not cease. // 313 //
To sever the bonds of saṃsāra, the ascetic should burn away both of these;
for through external thought and action, the increase of latent impressions (vāsanā) results from them.
Increasing through those two, it produces the cycle of existence for oneself;
and the means for the destruction of these three exists at all times and in all states. (315)
Through the observation of the measure of Brahman everywhere and from all sides,
and through the firmness of the latent impression of true being, that triad attains dissolution.
Upon the destruction of action, there occurs the destruction of thought; from this comes the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā).
The complete dissolution of latent impressions is liberation (mokṣa); that is held to be liberation while living (jīvanmukti). // 317 //
For when the manifestation of the latent impression of the Real (sadvāsanā) unfolds,
even this latent impression of "I" and so forth, though deeply ingrained, dissolves—
just as the light of the moon vanishes before the intense radiance of the rising sun.
It dissolves completely, just as darkness does. // 318 //
Just as the web of misfortunes consisting of darkness and its effects is no longer seen when the sun has risen,
so too [is it not seen] in the experience of the flavor of non-dual bliss.
There is neither bondage nor even the scent of suffering. // 319 //
Dissolving whatever is perceived as an object of sight and contemplating pure existence as a mass of bliss,
one remains concentrated, whether externally or internally.
One should pass the time when the bondage of karma still exists. // 320 //
"One must never be negligent regarding steadfastness in Brahman;
negligence is death—so said the Blessed One, the son of Brahmā. (321)
For the knower of his own true nature, there is no other misfortune than negligence;
from that comes delusion, from that the sense of "I," from that bondage, and from that suffering. (322)
Seeing even a wise man directed toward sense objects, forgetfulness distracts him with defects of the intellect, just as a woman distracts her beloved paramour.
Just as pulled-up moss does not remain for even a moment,
so too does Māyā envelop even a wise man who has turned his back on her.
If the mind, having deviated from its object, should even slightly fall outward toward this or that through negligence,
it is like a play-ball dropped from one's hand.
Just as one who has fallen upon a flight of stairs. // 325 //
When the mind enters into sense objects, it conceives of their qualities;
from right conceptualization arises desire, and from desire comes the impulse toward action in a person.
Therefore, for the discerning knower of Brahman, there is no death greater than negligence; when concentrated in samādhi,
he who is composed attains perfect success.
Be composed in soul and attentive. // 327 //
From that, there is a loss of one's true nature; having fallen away, one falls downward.
For one who has fallen, no ascent is seen again except through destruction.
Therefore, one should abandon volitional thought (*saṃkalpa*), for it is the cause of all misfortune;
he for whom there is liberation while living is alone liberated when bodiless.
The Yajurvedic scripture declares that fear arises for one who perceives even the slightest duality. (329)
Whenever this wise one perceives even an atom's worth of difference within the infinite Brahman, at that very moment he experiences fear.
That which was perceived as distinct due to negligence. // 330 //
He who forms the notion of "self" regarding this visible world— which is forbidden by hundreds of scriptural injunctions, traditional laws, and logical arguments—
enters into a succession of suffering upon suffering.
He who performs what is forbidden is like a thief. // 331 //
One who delights in truthful commitment and is liberated constantly attains his own greatness;
but one who delights in false commitment shall perish.
This very thing has been observed regarding those who are not thieves and those who are thieves.
Having abandoned the pursuit of the unreal, which is the cause of bondage,
the ascetic should remain established solely in the vision of the Self, thinking "I am this very [Self].
Indeed, does not the final realization in Brahman through one's own direct experience bring bliss?
It removes the suffering that is well-known as the effect of supreme ignorance. // 333 //
External attachment increases the fruit of evil tendencies even further; therefore,
having understood this through discernment, one should abandon the external.
One should constantly practice the contemplation of one's own true self.
When external objects are restrained, there is clarity of mind;
when the mind is clear, there is the vision of the Supreme Self;
when that is clearly seen, the bondage of worldly existence is destroyed.
The cessation of the external is the path to liberation. // 335 //
What wise person— discerning between the real and the unreal, relying on the authority of the scriptures, and perceiving the ultimate truth— would knowingly take recourse in what is non-existent?
Desiring liberation, he acts like a child for the sake of his own downfall. // 336 //
For one who is attached to the body and so forth, there is no liberation;
for one who is liberated, there is an absence of identification with the body and so forth.
As there is no waking for one who is asleep, nor sleep for one who is awake.
Dreams [do not apply] to those two, because they have different substrata for their qualities. // 337 //
