Having realized through the Self that one's own nature exists both within and without all moving and stationary beings as their underlying support,
and having abandoned all limiting adjuncts, one becomes of undivided form.
He who abides with his self fulfilled is liberated. // 338 //
There is nothing superior to the state of one's entire being as the cause for liberation from bondage;
this [liberation] occurs when there is no grasping at the visible world.
His entire being is always established in the Self. // 339 //
How indeed can the non-perception of the visible world be possible for one who dwells with the body as the self,

whose mind is intent upon the experience of external objects, and who performs various actions— [a state] which is [only] for those who have renounced all dharmas, rituals, and sense-objects, and who are solely devoted to the eternal Self?
This should be diligently performed within oneself by those who know reality and desire perpetual bliss.
For the sake of establishing the self of all, this Vedic revelation— "He is peaceful and self-controlled"— effects meditative absorption for the mendicant who has performed the rite of hearing.
The destruction of the "I-sense" (ahaṃkāra), whose power has been fully ascended, cannot be accomplished even suddenly by the wise,
unless they are steadfast in the samādhi known as the non-conceptual (nirvikalpa).
For these latent predispositions (vāsanās) indeed consist of endless and limitless existences. // 342 //
Having joined the person with the deluding power of the notion of "I" through the force of concealment (āvaraṇa),
the power of projection (vikṣepa-śakti) causes that person to be projected by means of the [material] qualities (guṇas).
The conquest of the power of distraction is difficult to achieve as long as there is no cessation of the power of concealment; for in the absence of that,
the distinction between the seer and the seen remains as indistinct as that between a lotus and water.
Then that obscuration in the self would vanish by its very nature; without doubt, one becomes free from obstruction,
for there is no longer any distraction if [the mind] is directed toward what is not false.
Right discernment, born of clear awakening,
cuts through the bond of delusion created by Māyā by analytically distinguishing the true nature of the categories of the seer and the seen.
For once liberated from that, there is no further cycle of existence. // 345 //
The fire of discernment between the higher and the lower burns away the entire thicket of ignorance;
for what seed of transmigration could possibly remain?
Of him who has fully attained the state of non-duality. // 346 //
For the cessation of obscuration occurs through the correct perception of reality;
there is the destruction of false knowledge and the removal of the suffering produced by its distractions. // 347 //

These three are seen [as illusory] through the correct knowledge of the true nature of the rope; therefore, the wise person seeking liberation from bondage should know the reality of the underlying substance.
Through its association with the Real, the intellect unfolds in the form of the mother and so forth, like iron through contact with fire;
since both of these are its effects, they are unreal.
It is seen in delusions, dreams, and mental fantasies. // 349 //
Therefore, all these transformations of primordial nature— beginning with the ego and ending with the body, as well as all objects of the senses—
are indeed subject to change from moment to moment.
But the self is never otherwise than non-existent. // 350 //
I am of the nature of eternal, non-dual, and indivisible consciousness alone;
the witness of the intellect and other faculties; distinct from both the existent and the non-existent; and the referent indicated by the notion of the word "I."
The supreme Self is directly manifest, a solid mass of eternal bliss. // 351 //
Thus, having distinguished between the real and the unreal,
and having ascertained the truth through the vision of his own awakening,
the wise man realizes his own Self as indivisible consciousness.
Being liberated from them, it subsides of its own accord. // 352 //
Then, through non-conceptual meditative absorption (samādhi), there occurs the complete dissolution of the knot of ignorance in the heart, when the vision of the non-dual Self arises. // 353 //
This conceptualization of "you," "I," and "this" arises from a defect of the intellect regarding the non-dual, undifferentiated Supreme Self;
all such mental construction ceases when one shines in meditative absorption.
One should attain dissolution through the ascertainment of the true nature of reality. // 354 //
The ascetic, peaceful, self-controlled, supremely withdrawn, and endowed with patience, constantly practicing meditative absorption, perceives his own universal nature; thereby,
he thoroughly burns away the conceptual constructions born from the darkness of ignorance.
Abiding in the form of Brahmā, he dwells in happiness, free from activity and free from conceptual construction. // 355 //
Those who, being concentrated, having dissolved the external world and the senses such as hearing, perceive their own mind as "I" within the conscious Self—
they alone are liberated from the bonds of the fetters of existence.
But others do not speak of things that are beyond the senses.
It appears divided only through the diversity of its limiting adjuncts; when those adjuncts are removed, it remains by itself alone.
Therefore, for the sake of dissolving the adjuncts, the wise man [should strive].
One should always abide in the steadfastness of meditative absorption for as long as an eon. // 357 //
A person attached to Being attains the state of Being through single-minded devotion;
for just as a worm meditating on a bee becomes fit for the state of a bee. // 358 //
Just as a worm, casting aside attachment to other activities and meditating on its state as a bee, attains the condition of a bee;
even so does the yogi [attain] the reality of the Supreme Self.
Having meditated, one arrives [at that state] through exclusive devotion to it alone. // 359 //
The reality of the supreme self is exceedingly subtle; it cannot be realized through gross vision,
but only by means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) with an extremely subtle mental function.
This should be understood by the noble ones whose intellects are exceedingly pure. // 360 //
Just as gold, purified by smelting in a crucible, abandons its impurities and attains its own inherent quality,
so too does the mind [abandon] the impurities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Having abandoned [the world] through meditative absorption, one attains reality. // 361 //
When the mind, thus ripened by the power of uninterrupted practice, merges into Brahman,
then there is the samādhi devoid of conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).
He is one who experiences by himself the taste of non-dual bliss. // 362 //
By means of this samādhi, there is the destruction of the entire knot of latent impressions and the annihilation of all karma,
both internally and externally, everywhere and at all times.
The manifestation of one's own true nature occurs effortlessly. // 363 //

One should know that reflection is a hundred times more effective than hearing; and nididhyāsana is a hundred-thousandfold more effective than reflection, while the state free from conceptual construction is infinite.
The reality of Brahman is certainly and clearly realized through non-conceptual meditative absorption;
not otherwise, because the movement of the mind is unstable.
It would become mixed with other conditions. // 365 //
Therefore, being self-controlled and with a tranquil mind, concentrate continuously upon the Inner Self;
destroy the darkness born of beginningless ignorance.
This has been accomplished through the contemplation of the oneness of all things. // 366 //
The first gateway to yoga is the restraint of speech, non-possessiveness, freedom from expectation, freedom from striving, and constant adherence to solitude. // 367 //

Abiding in solitude is the cause for the cessation of the senses; self-restraint is the means for the suppression of the mind; and through tranquility, the latent impression of egoism reaches dissolution.
By that, the yogi always experiences the unwavering bliss of Brahman.
Therefore, the sage must constantly exert effort toward the cessation of the mind alone. // 368 //
Restrain speech within the self; restrain that [self] within the intellect; and restrain the intellect within the witness of the intellect;
and that [witness] also within the perfect, non-conceptual Self.
Having dissolved [it], attain supreme peace. // 369 //
Through whichever limiting adjuncts—such as the body, vital breath, senses, mind, and intellect—the yogin’s activity is joined, he assumes the nature of that very thing. (370)

Through the cessation of that [conceptualization], the sage’s complete cessation of all [mental activity] is seen as bliss; it is the overwhelming experience of the essence of perpetual joy. // 371 //
Internal renunciation and external renunciation are appropriate only for one who is dispassionate;
indeed, it is the dispassionate person who, through the desire for liberation, abandons both internal and external attachments.
Only one who is truly dispassionate, being firmly established in Brahman, is able to abandon attachment to external objects as well as to internal states such as the ego.
O wise one, understand that for a person, detachment and awakening are like two wings;
they enable the ascent to the pinnacle of the mansion of liberation.
Without both of these, it is not accomplished by either one alone. // 374 //
For one possessed of absolute dispassion, there is meditative absorption;
for one who is absorbed, there is firm awakening;
and for one who has awakened to reality, there is liberation from bondage.
The liberated self experiences eternal bliss. // 375 //

I see nothing that generates greater happiness for one who has mastered the self than dispassion; and if that [dispassion] is accompanied by the most pure awakening of the Self, it yields the sovereignty of self-rule.
Since this is the door to the eternal maiden of liberation, you are superior to it.
Always being free from longing for anything else, always apply your wisdom toward your own self for the sake of the highest good. // 376 //
Cut off hope for these sense-objects which are like poison; this very thing is the work of Death.
Abandoning attachment to birth, family, and stage of life, cast ritual actions far away. Since the body and such are unreal, abandon the notion of a self; cultivate wisdom within the Self.
You are the seer, you are the unmanifest, you are the non-dual supreme Brahman, which is the reality in itself. // 377 //

Having firmly established the mind upon Brahman as the objective, having settled the external senses in their respective places, with the body motionless and remaining indifferent to its own physical state,
one attains the identity of Brahman and the self; and through that absorption, by means of an uninterrupted flow of consciousness, one remains thus perpetually.
One should joyfully drink the essence of the bliss of Brahman within oneself; what is the use of other things, which are utterly void? 378.
Abandoning the contemplation of non-self, which is a defilement and a cause of suffering, contemplate the Self, whose nature is bliss and which is the cause of liberation. // 379 //
This self-luminous witness of all, the sheath of pure consciousness, shines eternally,
having taken as its object this [world] which is distinct from the unreal.
Experience it as having the nature of an uninterrupted state of being.
One should clearly recognize this [reality] by means of an uninterrupted mode of being, devoid of any other cognitive conditions, as it is vividly manifest in its own essential nature.

Firmly establishing the absence of selfhood here, and relinquishing the "I" and so forth within [the body], one should remain indifferent toward them, like a clearly visible jar or other such objects. (382)
Having established the purified internal organ within its own nature— the Witness which is pure consciousness alone—
he gradually brings it to a state of immobility.
Then, one should gaze intently upon that very fullness.

One should contemplate the Self as being of an indivisible nature, liberated from all limiting adjuncts— such as the body, senses, vital breath, mind, and the sense of "I"— which are fashioned by one's own ignorance.
One should gaze upon it as being full, like the great expanse of space. // 384 //
Just as the single, pure sky remains undivided and does not become manifold, even when freed from hundreds of limiting conditions such as jars, pots, granaries, and needles; so too is the [Self].
It is one alone, liberated from the highest ego and so forth. // 385 //
All limiting adjuncts, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, are mere illusions;
therefore, one should perceive one's own Self as complete, abiding as the one Self. (386)
That which is imagined through delusion, upon its discernment,
is found to be merely that [delusion] itself and not distinct from it;
when delusion perishes, the reality as it has been perceived shines forth.
In the same way, the entire universe is the very nature of the Self, like the rope. // 387 //
He himself is Brahmā, he himself is Viṣṇu, he himself is Indra, he himself is Śiva;
he himself is this entire universe, and there is nothing whatsoever other than himself.
Within himself and also without himself, himself in front and himself behind;
himself indeed to the south and himself also to the north.
Likewise, one should also [visualize] oneself above and below. // 389 //
Just as everything— waves, foam, ripples, bubbles, and so forth— is in its true nature nothing but water,
so too this entire world, from the body to the sense of "I," is nothing but consciousness.
All is indeed consciousness alone, of a single flavor and pure. // 390 //

For one who stands at the ultimate limit of primordial nature, this entire world is understood as being only Being; there is nothing else existing apart from Being, which transcends both speech and mind.
What indeed is perceived as distinct from clay—the jar, the pot, the pitcher, and so forth?
Deluded by the intoxicant of illusion, he says, "I am you."
Where the scripture, by means of intensive repetition of action, declares "there is nothing else," it proclaims the absence of duality for the sake of ceasing false superimposition. (392)
Like space, it is pure and free from conceptual construction; it is boundless, motionless, and changeless;
empty within and without, non-dual, and without a second.
What supreme Brahman is there to be realized other than oneself? // 393 //
What more need be said here? In many ways it is taught that the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed Brahman itself;
this entire extended universe is Brahman, and the Veda declares Brahman to be non-dual.
Those of awakened intellect, having clearly renounced external objects, realize: "I am indeed Brahman."
Having become one with Brahman, they dwell perpetually as the self of constant consciousness and bliss; this is certain.

Thereafter, when the sheath composed of impurity has been forcibly cast off by the intellect awakened through the *ahaṃ* [mantra], and even the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*)— which resembles the wind— is likewise discarded,
one beholds that which is proclaimed in the Vedas as eternal fame and the embodiment of perpetual bliss.
Having recognized this as yourself, remain in the form of Brahman. // 395 //
As long as a person clings to the form of a corpse, he remains impure and a source of suffering for others— a dwelling place of birth, death, and disease;
but when he perceives the self as pure, auspicious in form, and immovable, [he attains liberation].
At that time, he indeed becomes liberated from them; for thus also says the Śruti.
By the elimination of all objects of appearance superimposed upon one's own self, one becomes the supreme Brahman itself—perfect, non-dual, and actionless. (397)
When the mental fluctuations have become stilled through meditative absorption,
no such conceptual construction is perceived within the non-conceptual Brahman, which is both the supreme self and the inner self.
For only mere verbal proliferation remains. // 398 //
This conceptual construction that "this universe exists" is a false imagination regarding a single reality;
since that reality is changeless, formless, and without distinction, whence can there be any differentiation? (399)
In that single reality which is empty of the states of seer, seeing, and the seen—unchanging, formless, and without distinction—from where could there be any duality? (400)
In that which is like the ocean at the end of an aeon—utterly full of a single reality, changeless, formless, and without distinction—from where could there be any duality? (401)
Where darkness, the cause of delusion, has dissolved as if into light within the non-dual, supreme reality that is devoid of distinctions—whence can there be duality? (402)
How could talk of duality reside in the supreme reality, which is of a single nature?
By whom has duality ever been perceived in the state of deep sleep, which consists of pure bliss? // 403 //
Indeed, the universe does not exist apart from the realization of the supreme reality within the eternally self-existent Brahman, which is free from conceptual construction;
nor is a snake perceived in a rope even when examined throughout the three periods of time.
For there is no drop of water in a mirage. // 404 //
"This duality is mere illusion; from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is non-dual"—thus the Śruti declares directly, and it is experienced in deep sleep. (405)
The non-difference of the superimposed from its substrate has been observed by the wise in cases such as the rope-snake; conceptual construction is sustained by delusion. (406)
This conceptual construction has its root in the mind; when the mind is absent, nothing at all exists.
Therefore, concentrate the mind upon the supreme self in its primordial form. 407
It is something of perpetual awakening, whose nature is absolute bliss, incomparable, transcendent, eternally liberated, and effortless;
it has the appearance of the boundless sky, partless, and free from conceptual construction.
The wise one contemplates the full Brahman within the heart during meditative absorption.
Devoid of both primordial nature and its transformations, a state transcending all mental cultivation, equal in flavor and beyond comparison, the mind is far removed from bondage;
established by the words of the Vedas, it is eternally well-known to us.
The wise one contemplates the full Brahman within the heart during meditative absorption.
It is of the nature of a reality devoid of the eight states, such as aging and death; resembling a mass of still water, it is beyond description,
with the modifications of the qualities (guṇas) stilled, eternal, peaceful, and one.
The wise one contemplates the full Brahman within the heart during meditative absorption.
With an internally concentrated mind, behold within your own nature the Self of unbroken majesty;
sever the bondage perfumed by the scent of worldly existence.
With effort, make your manhood fruitful!
Meditate upon the Self, which is free from all limiting adjuncts, being existence-consciousness-bliss and non-dual, abiding within yourself; you shall no longer be subject to the journey of saṃsāra.
Like a shadow of a man, perceived as a mere reflection through the experience of its fruit,
the body is cast away from afar like a corpse.
Furthermore, that Great-Souled One does not join this [to anything else]. // 413 //
Having attained the nature of eternal, stainless consciousness and bliss,
cast far away this limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of inert matter and impurity;
thereafter, let this vomited thing never be remembered again.
One contemplates that which has become the object of recollection for the sake of revulsion. // 414 //
Having completely incinerated this [world] along with its root in the fire of the eternally self-existent, non-conceptual Brahman,
one then becomes oneself the eternally pure awakening.
The most excellent knower abides as the very self of bliss. // 415 //
Whether the body, strung together by the thread of *prārabdha* karma, moves on or remains like a garland upon a cow,
the knower of reality does not behold it again.
One whose mental activity has dissolved into Brahman, which is the self consisting of bliss. // 416 //
Having realized the Self as indivisible bliss through its own true nature, what would the knower of reality desire, or for what purpose, that he should nourish this body? (417)
This, indeed, is the fruit for the perfected yogi who is liberated while living:
the constant tasting of the essence of bliss within the self, both externally and internally.
The fruit of dispassion is awakening; the fruit of awakening is cessation.
Peace arises from the experience of one's own bliss; this indeed is the fruit of cessation.
If there is an absence of each subsequent stage, then each preceding one is fruitless;
cessation is the supreme state, satisfaction, and an incomparable bliss that arises from itself.
Lack of revulsion toward suffering that has been directly perceived is the immediate fruit of knowledge:
how could a person, once possessed of discernment, ever perform those various loathsome actions that were committed during a time of delusion? (421)
The fruit of knowledge is the cessation of what is unreal,
while engagement [with it] is seen to be the fruit of ignorance;
this is observed in the case of one who knows and one who does not know regarding such things as a mirage.
Otherwise, what visible fruit for those who know could there be from this? // 422 //
If the knot of the heart consisting of ignorance has been destroyed without remainder, what indeed could be the cause for activity arising spontaneously in one who is free from desire? (423)
The non-arising of latent impressions regarding objects of enjoyment is the limit of dispassion;
the absence of the arising of the sense of "I" is the supreme limit of awakening. The non-origination of submerged mental fluctuations is the limit of the cessation of worldly boundaries. (424)
Always abiding in the form of Brahman, with an intellect liberated from external objects, perceiving this world like one who has awakened from a dream, like a child,
or like one who has seen a vision in sleep, he occasionally attains such wisdom that he no longer experiences the enjoyment of objects known by others.
There dwells some fortunate person who enjoys the fruit of infinite merit; he is to be honored on this earth.
This ascetic is one whose wisdom is established, who always enjoys bliss,
whose self is dissolved in Brahman alone, and who is changeless and free from action.

The modification of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpā*) and which penetrates the single nature of the purified Brahman and the Self—is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
He in whom this [wisdom] is firmly established is said to be one whose wisdom is steady (*sthitaprajña*). (427)
He whose wisdom is firmly established, whose bliss is uninterrupted, and for whom conceptual proliferation is almost entirely forgotten—he is considered liberated while living. // 428 //

He whose intellect is dissolved yet remains awake, who is devoid of the characteristics of the waking state, and whose awakening is free from latent impressions—he is considered liberated while living. // 429 //
He whose mental agitation regarding saṃsāra has been stilled, who, though possessing parts, is partless, and whose mind is free from anxiety—he is considered liberated while living. // 430 //
Even while this body continues to exist, following [the self] like a shadow,
the absence of the notions of "I" and "mine" is the characteristic of one liberated while living.
Non-attachment to the past, non-deliberation on the future, and even the attainment of equanimity—these are the characteristics of one liberated while living. // 432 //
Seeing with equanimity everywhere—in this world distinguished by merits and defects and inherently diverse—is the characteristic of one liberated while living. // 433 //

The characteristic of one liberated while living is the state of being unchanging in both circumstances, through equanimity of vision within oneself upon the attainment of desired and undesired objects. // 434 //

The characteristic of one liberated while living is the lack of awareness of both the internal and the external, due to the mind being absorbed in tasting the essence of the bliss of Brahman. // 435 //

He who remains in a state of indifference toward the body, the senses, and other such things that must be maintained, being free from the notions of "mine" and "I," possesses the characteristic of one liberated while living. // 436 //

He who, by the power of the scripture, has realized the state of Brahman as his own self and is completely liberated from the bondage of worldly existence, possesses the characteristics of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). // 437 //
He in whom neither the sense of "I" regarding the body and senses, nor the sense of "this" regarding anything other than that, arises anywhere, is considered liberated while living. // 438 //
He who, through wisdom, never perceives a difference between the inner self and Brahman, or between Brahman and the creation, possesses the characteristics of one liberated while living. // 439 //
He who maintains equanimity toward this [world] while it is being honored by the virtuous and oppressed by the wicked is characterized as one liberated while living. // 440 //
When sense-objects, impelled by others, enter therein like river currents into the ocean, they dissolve into pure being and do not produce any modification.
This ascetic, being liberated, brings them forth. // 441 //
For one who has realized the true nature of Brahman, there is no cyclic existence as before;
if such existence still persists, he has not truly realized the state of Brahman, for his mind remains directed toward the external.
If it is argued that this person wanders in saṃsāra due to the force of prior latent impressions (vāsanā), [we reply:
no, for those latent impressions are weakened by the realization of the oneness of Being.
Even for one who is excessively lustful, his impulse falters toward his mother;
likewise, for the wise man, it falters toward Brahman, the Knower of full bliss.
For one whose nature is that of profound contemplation (nididhyāsana), an external causal factor is observed;
the Śruti declares this to be "prārabdha" (the momentum of past karma) because its fruit is seen.
As long as there is the experience of pleasure and so forth, so long is prārabdha-karma held to exist;
for the arising of a fruit is preceded by action, and nowhere is it ever without action.
Through the realization "I am Brahman," that which has been accumulated over hundreds of millions of eons goes to destruction upon awakening, like the actions performed in a dream.
Whatever merit or intense evil is committed during the time of sleep—would that belong to one who has awakened from sleep for the sake of heaven or for hell? (448)
Having thoroughly realized one's own self to be unattached and indifferent, like the sky,
one is never clung to by any actions whatsoever, even those that are destined to come to pass.
Just as the sky is not stained by contact with a jar or by the fragrance of wine, so too the self is not stained at all by contact with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) or by their qualities. // 450 //
Action commenced prior to the arising of knowledge is not destroyed by that knowledge without having yielded its own fruit, like an arrow released toward a target. (451)
Once released with the thought that it was a tiger, the arrow does not stop even when [the target] is later seen to be a cow; with full force, it simply pierces the mark. (452)
Indeed, for the wise, accumulated karma is most powerful; its exhaustion occurs through experience, while its dissolution occurs through the fire of perfect knowledge.
But for those who, having realized the identity of Brahman and the Self, remain forever established in that state of oneness, there is no further rebirth.
For them, that triad does not exist anywhere at all; for them, it is only Brahman, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
For the sage who abides in the Self as the very Self of Brahman alone, devoid of identity with limiting adjuncts (upādhi),
the talk of the existence of *prārabdha* karma is not tenable.
It is like the discourse on the connection between objects and dreams for one who is awake. // 454 //
For one who is awakened does not exercise the sense of "I," "mine," or "this-ness" toward the body of appearances, nor even toward the phenomenal world that serves the functions of the body.
But he himself remains awake through vigilance. // 455 //
He has no desire to justify false objects,
nor is his gathering of the world seen to be for that purpose; if there were conformity to those false objects, it would be so.
It is certainly not maintained that he is free from sleep. // 456 //
In the same way, one who abides in the supreme Brahman remains as the self of pure being and perceives nothing else,
just as memory [remembers] an object seen in a dream.
Likewise, for one who knows thus, there is [the attainment of results] at the beginning of eating, releasing, and so forth. // 457 //
The body is fashioned by karma; let its *prārabdha* (commenced) portion be postulated.
However, it is not logical for the beginningless Self to be fashioned by karma, for the Self is certainly not produced by karma.
The Śruti, whose word is unfailing, declares that he is unborn, eternal, and everlasting;
for one who abides as the Self in that state, how can there be any conception of *prārabdha* (the momentum of past actions)?
Prārabdha succeeds only so long as there is the persistence of the notion that the body is the self;
since the identification of the body with the self is no longer desired, one should therefore abandon prārabdha.

Indeed, even the conceptualization of a "commenced" (prārabdha) karma for the body is nothing but an illusion; for how can there be existence for that which is superimposed? How can there be birth for that which is unreal?
How can there be destruction for that which is unborn? And how can there be a "commenced" karma for that which is non-existent? (461)
For those dull-witted people who harbor the doubt: "If through knowledge the effects of ignorance are dissolved along with their root, how can this body remain? (462)
The Śruti declares that the external world was begun for the purpose of concentration through outward perception,
and not for the sake of teaching the reality of the body and so forth to the wise.
Brahman alone is entirely full, without beginning or end, immeasurable, and immutable; it is one without a second, and there is no diversity whatsoever here. 464.
Brahman alone is the true multitude, the mass of consciousness, eternally the mass of bliss, and actionless; it is one and non-dual, and there is no diversity whatsoever here. 465.
The innermost essence, full, infinite, facing every direction, Brahman is indeed one and non-dual; there is no diversity whatsoever here. (466)
Brahman alone is that which is not to be abandoned, not to be taken up, not to be grasped, and without support; it is one and non-dual; there is no diversity whatsoever here. 467.
Brahman is devoid of qualities, partless, subtle, free from conceptual construction, and stainless; it is one alone, without a second, and there is no diversity whatsoever here. 468.
That whose essential nature cannot be defined and which is beyond the reach of mind and speech—Brahman alone is non-dual; here there is no diversity whatsoever. (469)
Brahman alone is truly existent, self-established, pure, awakened, and peerless; it is one without a second, and there is no duality whatsoever here. 470.
Having cast off passion and utterly abandoned enjoyments, those great ascetics— peaceful and well-subdued—
having realized this supreme reality at the end, [attain liberation].
They have attained supreme bliss through the yoga of the self. // 471 //
You too, having reflected upon this supreme reality as the very nature of the self— a mass of bliss—
should dispel the delusion imagined by your own mind.
May he be liberated, his purpose accomplished, and awakened. // 472 //
Behold the reality of the self with the eye of clear awakening through a concentration that is perfectly steady;
for if it is correctly observed, there will be no doubt.
An object that has been heard is not conceptualized again. // 473 //
Upon attaining the Self, which is of the nature of truth, knowledge, and bliss, through liberation from the bondage of one's own ignorance,
the scripture, reasoning, and the teacher’s instruction serve as the means of valid knowledge.
And one's own internal experience, established within, is the means of valid cognition. // 474 //
Bondage, liberation, satisfaction, anxiety, health, hunger, and so forth are to be known by oneself alone; whereas the knowledge of others is merely inferential. (475)
The teachers, like the Vedas, awaken one from a distance;
the wise man should cross over by means of wisdom alone, which is graced by the Lord.
Having known his own unfragmented Self by means of his own direct experience,
the perfected one stands face-to-face within himself as the non-conceptual Self.
This is the definitive explanation of the Vedānta tenet:
the individual soul and the entire universe are indeed Brahman;
liberation is simply the state of abiding in the undivided form.
The Śruti scriptures are the authority regarding the non-dual Brahman. // 478 //
Thus, having understood the supreme reality through the words of the Guru and the authority of the Vedas, and by means of his own reasoning,
he whose senses were stilled remained with a concentrated mind.
In some places, he appeared with the form of a mountain due to his steadfastness in the self. // 479 //
Having composed his mind upon the Supreme Brahman for some time,
he arose from that supreme bliss and spoke these words.
The intellect is destroyed and worldly activity has dissolved through the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self;
I do not know this, nor do I know that which is not this.
Or what happiness exists, or how much, that is without limit? // 481 //
The majesty of the ocean of the Supreme Brahman, filled with the flood of the nectar of its own bliss, cannot indeed be described by speech nor can it be conceived by the mind;
may my mind attain the state of a stone that has been weathered by the rains upon the shore of the great ocean.
In a mere fraction of a fraction of which, one is now dissolved in bliss and becomes tranquil through the nature of supreme joy. // 482 //
Where has this world gone, or by whom was it taken away, and where is it hidden?
Just now it was seen by me, and now it is not—what a great marvel!
What is to be abandoned, what is to be accepted, what else is there, or what is distinct, within the great ocean of Brahman, which is filled with the nectar of indivisible bliss? (484)
I see nothing here, I hear nothing, and I know nothing;
by my very self, in the form of eternal bliss, I am distinct from all this.
Homage, homage to you, the Great-Souled Guru,
who is liberated from attachment, the most excellent of beings,
whose very nature is the essence of eternal non-dual bliss.
To the vast one, whose ocean of compassion is forever boundless. // 486 //
I, whose exhaustion born of the heat of worldly existence was dispelled by the descent of the thick moonlight from the moon of your sidelong glance,
have attained unbroken majesty.
In an instant, he attains the state of Nanda, the inexhaustible abode of the self. // 487 //
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, I am liberated from the grasp of worldly existence; by your grace, I am of the nature of eternal bliss and I am full. (488)
I am unattached, I am bodiless, I am signless, I am indestructible;
I am perfectly tranquil, I am infinite, I am stainless, and I am the eternal one. // 489 //
I am the non-doer, I am the non-enjoyer, I am changeless and actionless;
I am the very nature of pure consciousness, I am the absolute, the eternally auspicious one.
I am indeed distinct from the seer, the hearer, the speaker, the doer, and the enjoyer; my nature is eternal, uninterrupted, actionless, limitless, unattached, and perfect consciousness. // 491 //
"I am not this, nor am I that; I am the supreme, pure illuminator of both.
Empty of exterior and interior, full, I am indeed the non-dual Brahman. // 492 //

I am indeed that non-dual Brahman—the incomparable, beginningless reality, far removed from the conceptualizations of "you," "I," "this," or "that"—the truth which is the singular essence of eternal bliss. 493.
I am Nārāyaṇa; I am the destroyer of hell; I am the destroyer of the cities [of the demons]; I am the Supreme Person, the Lord;
I am unbroken consciousness, the witness of all without exception.
I am without a lord, without the sense of "I," and without the sense of "mine."
I alone abide in all beings as the self of knowledge, being the internal and external support;
I myself am both the enjoyer and the entirety of that which is enjoyed.
Whatever was previously perceived as distinct through the notion of "this-ness. // 495 //
In me, the ocean of unbroken bliss, the waves of the universe arise and dissolve in manifold ways through the agitation of the winds of illusion.
The states of grossness and so forth have been imagined in me through delusion and superimposed by people due to their constant mental projection,
just as the years of a kalpa are projected upon time.
The seasons and so forth are within the partless and non-conceptual. // 497 //
That which has been planted shall never become a defiler of its support by the foolish who are corrupted by extreme faults;
it does not moisten a region of saline soil.
The great torrent of water in a mirage. // 498 //
Like space, I am far removed from all smearing;
like the sun, I am distinct from all that is luminous;
like a mountain, I am eternally immovable.
Like the ocean, I am devoid of a further shore. // 499 //
I have no connection with the body, just as the sky has none with a cloud;
therefore, how could those states—waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—be my attributes?
It is that very same adjunct (upādhi) which comes and goes; it is that very same one which performs actions and experiences their results;
it is that very same one which, growing old, dies—this is always "I."
He remains perfectly immovable, like a mountain of noble lineage. // 501 //
For me there is neither engagement nor cessation, for I am eternally of one form, partless,
unitary, dense, and continuous.
How indeed can he who is full like space engage in activity?
Whence can there be merit or sin for me— who am devoid of sense organs, devoid of consciousness, devoid of transformation, and devoid of form— since I am the experience of unbroken bliss?
For the Śruti also declares that it is "unapproached. // 503 //
Whether touched by shade or heat, or whether it be cold or pleasant, or even unpleasant—whatever it may be—it does not at all touch that person who is distinct from it. (504)
The attributes of the witness do not touch the witness, who is distinct from them—
unchanging and indifferent— just as the conditions of a house do not affect a lamp.
Just as fire has the status of a witness with respect to an action, just as it possesses the power to determine burning,
and just as a rope has a connection with the object superimposed upon it.
In the very same way, it is so for me, whose nature is the immutably abiding consciousness-self.
Neither am I the doer nor the one who causes to do; neither am I the enjoyer nor the one who causes to enjoy;
neither am I the seer nor the one who causes to see.
Thus, I am the self-luminous one, whose nature is unlike anything else.
When the limiting adjunct moves, the flickering of the reflection is perceived as belonging to it;
yet those of deluded intellect fail to realize that the original source,
like the sun, is actually devoid of action.
"I am the doer," "I am the enjoyer," "I am slain"—thus [one thinks]. // 508 //
Whether it rolls in water or on land, this inert thing may do as it pleases; I am not defiled by its qualities, just as the sky is not affected by the qualities of a jar.
Agency, enjoyership,
wickedness, intoxication, insentience, bondage, liberation, and so forth—
these are conceptual constructions of the intellect, but they do not exist in reality.
In one's own self, in the supreme Brahman, which is absolute and non-dual. // 510 //

Let there be transformations of primordial nature tenfold, hundredfold, or even thousandfold; what does it matter to me, whose mind is free from attachment? A dense cloud never touches the sky anywhere.
This entire universe, from the unmanifest up to the gross, is perceived therein as a mere appearance;
it is subtle like space, devoid of beginning or end.
I am that very non-duality which is Brahman. // 512 //
The support of all, the illuminator of all things,
possessing all forms, omnipresent, entirely empty,
eternal, pure, immovable, and free from conceptual construction.
I am that very non-duality which is Brahman. // 513 //
That which has cast off all particularities of māyā, whose nature is ever-fresh, which is not to be reached by the means of cognition, and whose form is truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss.
I am that very non-duality which is Brahman. // 514 //
I am actionless, I am changeless, I am partless, I am formless;
I am free from conceptual construction, I am eternal.
I am without support and free from duality. // 515 //
I am the self of all, I am all, I am beyond all, I am non-dual; I am absolute, indivisible awakening, I am bliss, I am uninterrupted. // 516 //
This sovereign glory of self-rule and universal empire has been attained by me through the grace and majesty of your compassionate fortune; [I offer it] to the great-souled Śrī Guru.
Homage, homage be to you; again, homage be to you! // 517 //

With extreme compassion for this one who wanders and suffers daily through manifold torments in the dense forest of birth, old age, and death created by illusion— a great dream— afflicted by the tiger of ego-clinging.
O Guru, having awakened me from deep sleep, you have made me understand the supreme reality.
Salutations to that certain unique light, ever one; salutations, O King of Gurus, to you who shine forth in the form of the universe! 519.
Thus, having observed his excellent disciple—
who had attained the bliss of the Self, awakened to reality,
and whose heart was filled with joy— that lord of teachers [spoke].
Furthermore, that Great-Souled One spoke these supreme words: // 520 //

The world is thus a continuous stream of perceptions of Brahman; therefore, with a tranquil mind, one should perceive everything everywhere as Brahman alone through the vision of the inner self, even in all states of being.
What else besides form is seen by those with sight when looking all around?
In the same way, for one who is a knower of Brahman, what else could there be as a locus for the mind's dwelling? (521)
Abandoning that experience of the essence of supreme bliss, what wise man would take delight in empty things while the moon, so intensely gladdening, shines forth?
Who would wish to look upon the moon of the mind? // 522 //
Indeed, there is no satisfaction nor any destruction of suffering through the experience of unreal objects; rather,
[satisfaction arises] from the experience of the essence of non-dual bliss.
Satisfied, remain always in happiness through steadfastness in the Self.
Seeing only yourself in every way, considering yourself as non-dual, and experiencing your own bliss, pass your time, O Great-minded One. (524)
Conceptualization within the non-conceptual Self of unbroken awareness is like imagining cities in the sky; therefore,
one should always abide as that Self which consists of non-dual bliss.
Having attained supreme peace, practice silence.

Silent abiding is the supreme tranquility for the great-souled knower of Brahman, whose intellect is free from the cause of conceptual constructions that are like unreal fictions, and who has realized the Self as Brahman.
Wherein there is the uninterrupted bliss of non-dual joy. // 526 //

For one who has realized the true nature of the Self and drinks the essence of its own bliss, there is no higher source of supreme happiness than the silence born of the absence of latent impressions.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or otherwise,
the wise sage who always delights in the self may dress as he pleases.
For the great-souled one who has perfected reality, there is no activity hindered by dependence on place, time, posture, direction, space, or the objects of perception and so forth.
In self-awareness, what need is there for conditions such as restriction? // 529 //
What rule does one observe in order to cognize "this is a jar," such that, in its presence, the cognition of the object occurs, even without the excellence of a means of valid cognition? (530)
This self is eternally established; it manifests when there is a means of valid cognition, and it does not depend upon place, nor time, nor even purity.
Just as the cognition "I am Devadatta" is independent [of external objects], so too for the knower of Brahman is the realization "I am Brahman. (532)
Since the entire world shines by his splendor like the sun, what indeed could possibly illuminate him—who is without self, non-existent, and insubstantial? (533)
What indeed could illuminate that knower by whom the Vedas, the Shastras, the Puranas, and all living beings become meaningful? (534)
This Self is self-luminous, possessed of infinite power, immeasurable, and the experience of all;
by knowing this very one, one is liberated from bondage.
Victorious is this most excellent among the supreme knowers of Brahman! // 535 //
He is neither weary nor delighted by sense objects;
he neither clings nor becomes dispassionate,
but always sports and rejoices in himself.
Satisfied by the essence of uninterrupted bliss. // 536 //
Having abandoned hunger and bodily pain, a child plays with objects;
in the same way, the wise man, free from "mine-ness" and "I-ness," rejoices in happiness.
Alms obtained without anxiety or dejection as food; drinking from the waters of rivers; a state of independence and unrestrained freedom; fearless sleep in cremation grounds or forests;
clothing consisting of the quarters of space, free from washing or drying; and the earth as a bed.
The movement of the wise is through the streets of the Upanishads; their play is in the Supreme Brahman.
Supporting this body as if it were a celestial chariot,
the knower of the Self enjoys all the objects presented before him according to another's will, like a child.
He whose outward signs are unmanifest and who is not attached to external things. // 539 //
Whether naked or clothed,
or even wearing only a skin, he abides in the sky of consciousness;
like a madman or like a child.
Or else he wanders upon the earth like a piśāca. // 540 //
Free from desires and having transcended the form of desire, the sage wanders alone;
always satisfied with his own self, he abides by himself as the Self of all.

In one place a fool, in another a scholar; in one place possessing the splendor of a great king, in another wandering as a gentle ascetic; in one place adopting the behavior of a python, in another becoming a worthy recipient of offerings, in another being held in contempt, and in yet another remaining unknown.
Thus the wise one conducts himself, constantly blissful with supreme joy. // 542 //
Though penniless, he is always content; though without companions, he possesses great strength;
though eternally satisfied, he does not eat; and being peerless, he views all things with equanimity.
Though performing actions or not performing them, he is a non-enjoyer even while being the enjoyer of fruits; though possessing a body, he is bodiless; and though limited, he is all-pervading.
Neither pleasure nor pain, nor likewise good fortune or misfortune, ever touch this knower of Brahman, who is eternally bodiless.
Happiness and suffering, as well as merit and demerit, belong to the conceited one who possesses connections with gross objects and the like;
they do not belong to the sage, the true Self, whose bonds have been shattered.
Whence could there be either a pleasant or an unpleasant fruit? // 546 //

Because its light appears as if swallowed by darkness, the sun, though not actually swallowed, is said by people to be "swallowed" due to delusion, for in ignorance one does not recognize the true nature of things. (547)

In the same way, the ignorant perceive the best of knowers of Brahman—who is liberated from the bonds of the body and so forth—as if he still possessed a body, because they see only the appearance of a body. (548)
Just as a snake remains within its slough after casting it off, so does this [self] remain within the body,
being moved here and there by whatever vital breath (prāṇavāyu).
Just as a piece of wood is carried by a current over low and high ground,
so too is the body led by destiny through experiences appropriate to the time.
One whose body is liberated moves among enjoyments like a worldly being due to the latent impressions fashioned by prārabdha-karma;
yet the perfected one dwells here himself in silence, like a witness.
Like the hub of a wheel, it is empty of conceptual construction and discursive thought. // 551 //
Established in the characteristic of pure perception, he neither engages the senses with their objects nor withdraws them from them;
nor does he even slightly look toward the fruit of action.
His mind is utterly intoxicated by drinking the essence of the dense nectar of his own bliss. // 552 //
Having abandoned the movement between the perceptible and the imperceptible, he who remains as the solitary Self is himself Śiva manifest; he is the supreme knower of Brahman. // 553 //
Even while living, he is forever liberated, having achieved his purpose as the best among the knowers of Brahman;
through the destruction of limiting adjuncts, being Brahman itself, he attains the non-dual Brahman.
Just as an actor remains the same man whether in costume or out of it, so too the supreme knower of Brahman is always Brahman alone and nothing else. // 555 //
Wherever the body of the ascetic who has become one with Brahman may fall, shattered like a leaf from a tree, it has already been consumed by the fire of consciousness.
For the sage who always abides in the Self, which is Brahman, as one whose nature is ever full, non-dual bliss,
there is no waiting for the appropriate time or place.
For the purpose of casting off this mass of skin, flesh, and excrement. // 557 //
Liberation is not the liberation of the body, nor of the staff, nor of the water-pot;
rather, liberation is the release from the knot of ignorance in the heart, because it is for that reason [that one is liberated]. (558)
Whether it falls into a canal, a river, a sacred field, or even at a crossroads—if a leaf falls, does that bring any good or evil to the tree? (559)
Just as there is the destruction of a leaf, a flower, or a fruit, so too is there the destruction of the body, the senses, the vital breaths, and the intellect;
but there is no destruction whatsoever of one's own Self, which is eternally existent by nature.
And this exists like a tree, having the form of Nanda. // 560 //

Having restated the definition of the Self as "a mass of consciousness," which indicates its true nature, [the scriptures] describe the destruction of that which is merely conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi). 561.
The scripture declares the indestructibility of the Self: "Verily, this Self is indeed imperishable," even while perishable modifications are passing away. (562)
Just as stones, trees, grass, grain, chaff, and the like, when burned, become nothing but earth, even so do the body,
senses, life-breaths, mind, and all other objects of perception.
Burnt by the fire of knowledge, it attains the state of the supreme Self.
Just as darkness, being of a different nature, dissolves into the light of the sun,
even so the entire visible world dissolves into Brahman.
Just as when a jar is destroyed, the space within clearly becomes the universal space itself,
so too upon the dissolution of limiting adjuncts, the knower of Brahman himself becomes Brahman alone.
Just as milk poured into milk, oil into oil, or water into water becomes one through their union, so does the sage who knows the Self become one with the Self.
Thus, having attained the state of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*), the indivisible nature of pure existence (*sanmātratva*),
and the state of Brahman, this ascetic does not return again.

For that person whose body of ignorance and so forth has been consumed by the knowledge of the eternal unity of the Self, there is no arising from Brahman, because he has become Brahman itself. // 568 //

In the construction of an illusion, bondage and liberation do not exist in reality within one's own self, just as there is neither the appearance nor the departure of a snake from a motionless rope. (569)
Bondage and liberation must be described in terms of the existence or non-existence of obscuration;
yet there is no obscuration whatsoever belonging to Brahman, because nothing else exists, and thus it is unobscured.
If such obscuration were to exist, there would be a loss of non-duality, for the Śruti does not tolerate duality. (570)
Fools falsely imagine bondage and liberation as qualities of the intellect within the Reality,
just as one might imagine an obscuration of the sun caused by clouds.
Since this imperishable is non-dual, unattached consciousness. // 571 //
The notions that "it exists" and "it does not exist" with respect to an object are merely qualities of the intellect; they do not belong to an eternal entity.

Therefore, bondage and liberation are fashioned by illusion and do not exist in the Self; for how could there be any conceptual construction regarding that supreme reality, which is partless, actionless, tranquil, faultless, stainless, and non-dual, like the sky? (573)
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one bound nor a practitioner, neither one seeking liberation nor one liberated— this is the ultimate truth.
Today I have revealed to you this supreme and most secret essence, which is the established conclusion within the heart of all the Vedas;
it is free from the defects of the Kali age and intended for one whose intellect is liberated from desire.
Having repeatedly meditated upon you as one who desires liberation, like one's own son... [575]
Having heard these words of the teacher, he bowed with humility;
permitted by him, he departed, freed from his bonds.
With his mind perpetually immersed in the ocean of eternal bliss, the Guru wandered incessantly, purifying the entire earth.
Thus, through the dialogue between the teacher and the disciple, the definition of the Self has been established for the sake of easily understanding the truth by those seeking liberation. // 578 //
May those who have eliminated all mental defects through their practice, who are detached from the pleasures of existence, and whose minds are tranquil, honor this beneficial instruction.
Those ascetics who delight in sacred learning and are seekers of liberation.
For those weary from the agony of burning heat produced by the rays of the sun of suffering on the path of saṃsāra, wandering aimlessly in the desert land out of a thirst for water,
[the Guru] reveals the non-dual Brahman— the source of bliss and a nectar-ocean situated very near.
This speech of Śaṅkara, which bestows liberation, is triumphant. // 580 //
Thus ends the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi composed by Śaṅkarācārya.
Oṃ tat sat.
